a_rows_sample.anchor: What can KnowledgeOS legitimately know? ... What may KnowledgeOS legitimately do with what it knows? ... Knowledge\neq Decision\neq Action
a_rows_sample.statement: States the pivot from epistemology to action: Knowledge ≠ Decision ≠ Action.

a_rows_sample.anchor: World\rightarrow Observation\rightarrow Evidence\rightarrow Knowledge\rightarrow Decision\rightarrow Action\rightarrow World ... K_t\rightarrow D_t\rightarrow A_t\rightarrow W_{t+1}\rightarrow K_{t+1} ... the beginning of a genuine epistemic control system
a_rows_sample.statement: Formulates the architecture as a closed control loop with time-indexed transitions K_t->D_t->A_t->W_{t+1}->K_{t+1}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(Y\mid X)\neq P(Y\mid do(X)) in general ... the fundamental distinction between observation and intervention
a_rows_sample.statement: States the central distinction P(Y|X) ≠ P(Y|do(X)) in general, the fundamental distinction between observation and intervention.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(Failure\mid Deployment)=0.10 ... cannot automatically conclude P(Failure\mid do(Deployment))=0.10 ... deployments may happen under special circumstances ... observational statistics can be confounded
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: observational deployment-failure statistics may be confounded (experienced engineers deploying during stable periods vs risky emergency deployments), so observational and interventional probabilities can diverge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: M=(V,E) ... Traffic->Load->Failure Risk<-Deployment ... an intervention can be evaluated against the model
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked causal-graph example (Traffic->Load, Deployment->Failure Risk) enabling intervention evaluation against an explicit model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Action=Intentional change to the world ... The distinction between Event and Intervention must remain explicit
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Action as intentional change to the world, kept explicitly distinct from a mere Event.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Action=(ActionID,Intent,Target,Preconditions,ExpectedEffects,Risk,Authorization,Reversibility,MonitoringPlan) ... much richer than execute(command)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a nine-field Action domain object, much richer than a bare execute(command).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Why are we doing this? ... Intent=ReduceSecurityRisk ... the same technical action can have different meanings under different contexts
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires every significant action to carry an explicit Intent, since the same technical action can carry different meanings under different contexts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Preconditions(Action) must hold ... Execute(A) is allowed only if \bigwedge_i P_i=True
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines preconditions as a conjunctive gate on execution (e.g. Approved(Change), BackupAvailable, RollbackPossible, MaintenanceWindowOpen).

a_rows_sample.anchor: ActionAuthorization=ProofOfRequiredPreconditions ... connects directly to 25T ... a powerful unification
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes action authorization as proof of required preconditions, explicitly connecting to Step 25T's proof-obligation machinery — 'a powerful unification.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Recommended(Action) does not imply Authorized(Action) ... Authorized(Action) does not imply Recommended(Action) ... independent dimensions
a_rows_sample.statement: States Recommendation and Authorization are independent dimensions, neither implying the other.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision=(Options,Evidence,Constraints,ExpectedUtility,Risk,SelectedAction,Rationale) ... a structured epistemic object
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a seven-field Decision object as a structured epistemic object.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EU(a)=\sum_s P(s\mid K)U(a,s) ... requires explicit utility assumptions
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines expected utility EU(a)=sum_s P(s|K)U(a,s), requiring explicit utility assumptions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Utility(a) ... no universal ... U(a,s\mid Context) ... maximize availability may conflict with minimize security risk ... Utility belongs to the decision context
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a universal Utility(a), requiring context-relative U(a,s|Context), worked with a conflicting-objectives example.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Risk(a)=P(Loss\mid a)\times Impact(Loss) ... Risk(a)=\sum_i P(L_i\mid a)C(L_i) ... still incomplete when tail risks matter; dependencies are nonlinear; consequences are irreversible
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a simple multi-scenario risk model, flagged as still incomplete under tail risk, nonlinear dependency, or irreversibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(CatastrophicFailure)=0.001 ... naive expected-value calculation may make the action look acceptable ... governance may require NoGo ... ExpectedUtility does not replace risk policy
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked tail-risk example showing expected-value reasoning can wrongly appear acceptable, requiring governance's separate authority to mandate NoGo — 'ExpectedUtility does not replace risk policy.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: RiskTolerance(Context) ... Risk(a)\le RiskTolerance may be required ... extremely strict [threshold] for critical operations
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines domain-set RiskTolerance(Context) as a required threshold gate, stricter for critical operations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Reversible or Irreversible ... Restart service highly reversible ... Database migration potentially reversible ... Deletion of evidence potentially irreversible
a_rows_sample.statement: Classifies actions along a Reversible/Irreversible spectrum, worked with three examples of differing reversibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Risk(A\mid Rollback)<Risk(A) ... rollback itself must be tested ... RollbackPossible must itself be evidence-backed. A common engineering mistake is we can always roll back. Not necessarily
a_rows_sample.statement: States reversibility can lower effective risk (Risk(A|Rollback)<Risk(A)), but warns 'we can always roll back' is a common engineering mistake — RollbackPossible must itself be evidence-backed, illustrated by irreversible database migration information loss.

a_rows_sample.anchor: BlastRadius(A)=AffectedEntities+AffectedCapabilities+AffectedUsers+AffectedProcesses ... a small-probability failure with enormous blast radius may require stronger controls
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines BlastRadius(A) compositionally, noting a small-probability but enormous-blast-radius failure may require stronger controls.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Knowledge 
eq Goal 
eq Decision 
eq Action 
eq Outcome and A good decision is not necessarily the action with the highest probability of success. It depends on purpose, utility, risk, constraints, authority, reversibility and uncertainty.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the governing five-way separation Knowledge≠Goal≠Decision≠Action≠Outcome, and that a good decision is not the highest-success-probability action — it depends on purpose, utility, risk, constraints, authority, reversibility, and uncertainty.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental problem ... Nexus 3.69 is old and should be upgraded. That is knowledge. It does not yet imply: Upgrade Nexus now. What is the goal? What is the desired outcome? What constraints apply? What risks exist? What alternatives exist? Who is authorized? Is the action reversible? What is th
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues knowledge alone does not determine action, listing nine questions (goal, outcome, constraints, risks, alternatives, authority, reversibility, cost, do-nothing baseline) that must be answered first.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Goal ... G=(GoalID,DesiredState,Purpose,Scope,Priority,Constraints,Deadline,Authority). Maintain a supported Nexus repository service without unacceptable production disruption. This is much richer than "Upgrade Nexus." The latter is an action. The former is a goal. ... Goal versus Ideal State ... G
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Goal=(GoalID,DesiredState,Purpose,Scope,Priority,Constraints,Deadline,Authority), distinguishing it from a mere action ('upgrade Nexus') and from IdealState (Goal→IdealState but Goal≠IdealState).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Goal as intentional direction ... G:CurrentState\rightarrow DesiredState. The goal establishes the direction of change. ... Multiple goals ... G_1=Upgrade, G_2=MinimizeDowntime, G_3=MinimizeCost, G_4=MaintainCompliance. These goals can conflict. \mathcal G=\{G_1,G_2,\ldots,G_n\}. ... Goal priority .
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a goal set G={G1,...,Gn} that can genuinely conflict (worked with four competing example goals), requiring explicit GoalConflict detection rather than silently optimizing one while pretending both were achieved; Priority≠Truth (normative/organizational).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Intention ... A goal says: What do we want? An intention says: What are we currently committed to pursuing? Intention = CommitmentToGoalOrPlan. Goal: UpgradeNexus. Intention: PerformControlledMigrationAfterApproval.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Intention=CommitmentToGoalOrPlan, distinct from a Goal ('what we want' vs 'what we're currently committed to pursuing').

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision ... D: \mathcal A\rightarrow a^* under a specified decision model. ... include a_0=NoAction. a^*\in\mathcal A\cup\{NoAction\}. ... Decision versus Action ... We choose to migrate Nexus. versus Execute migration procedure. Decision\neq Action. A decision can exist without execution.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Decision D:A→a* including an explicit NoAction option, distinguishing Decision (choosing) from Action (executing) — Decision ≠ Action, a decision can exist without execution.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Authorization ... Authorized(D,Authority,Context,t). Decision=UpgradeNexus may be technically sound but Authorized=False. Then execution is prohibited.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Authorized(D,Authority,Context,t) as a separate gate — a technically sound decision may still be unauthorized, prohibiting execution.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Action representation ... A=(ActionID,Preconditions,Operation,ExpectedEffects,Resources,Constraints,RiskProfile,Reversibility,AuthorityRequirement). An action therefore has a semantic contract.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Action=(ActionID,Preconditions,Operation,ExpectedEffects,Resources,Constraints,RiskProfile,Reversibility,AuthorityRequirement) as a semantic contract.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Preconditions ... BackupAvailable, MigrationPlanApproved, TargetEnvironmentReady. Pre(A,K)=True must hold before execution. If Pre(A,K)=Unknown, we should not pretend it is satisfied. ... Effects ... Effects(A,S)\rightarrow S'. Action: S_t\rightarrow S_{t+1}. This connects directly to Step 16. ... E
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Pre(A,K) preconditions (three example requirements) never pretended satisfied when Unknown, action effects as a state transition connecting to Step 16, and ExpectedEffect ≠ GuaranteedEffect (some actions deterministic, others probabilistic P(S'|A,S)).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Outcome ... Outcome=ObservedResult(Action). Expected: Nexus upgraded successfully. Actual: Upgrade completed but repository synchronization failed. The outcome is new evidence. ... Closed action loop ... Knowledge \rightarrow Decision \rightarrow Action \rightarrow Outcome \rightarrow Observation \r
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Outcome=ObservedResult(Action) as new evidence, worked with an expected-vs-actual mismatch example, closing the loop Knowledge→Decision→Action→Outcome→Observation→Knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Utility ... U(a,s) the utility of action a if state s occurs. Utility may include business value; reliability; cost; time; risk; compliance; maintainability; strategic value. ... Utility is not truth ... A highly useful action is not necessarily "more true." Utility\neq Truth. Utility belongs to dec
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Utility U(a,s) over eight example dimensions, states Utility≠Truth, and defines expected utility EU(a|K)=E[U(a,S)|K].

b_rows_sample.anchor: Risk ... Risk(a,s)=Impact(a,s)\times Likelihood(s\mid a). But this is appropriate only where probability is justified. More generally Risk = f(Impact,Likelihood,Uncertainty,Exposure,Reversibility). ... Risk versus uncertainty ... HighRisk because Impact=Extreme even when Likelihood=Unknown. Unknown
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Risk=f(Impact,Likelihood,Uncertainty,Exposure,Reversibility), warning Unknown likelihood does not imply Low risk — extreme impact alone can produce high risk regardless of unknown likelihood.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Reversibility ... DeployReversibleConfiguration versus DeleteProductionData. The second has far greater consequence if wrong. Reversibility must be a first-class action property. ... Irreversibility ... Irrev(a)\in[0,1] ... but this should not necessarily be the universal scalar representation. It m
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires Reversibility be a first-class action property (worked with a reversible-config vs delete-production-data contrast), preferring a structured ReversibilityProfile over a single scalar Irrev(a)∈[0,1].

b_rows_sample.anchor: Constraints ... Valid(a,K) \iff \forall c\in\mathcal C: c(a,K)=True. If a critical constraint is False, the action is invalid. If it is Unknown, the action may be undecidable. ... Hard versus soft constraints ... Hard constraint Must not be violated. Soft constraint Prefer not to violate. HardConstr
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines action validity Valid(a,K)=∀c∈C:c(a,K)=True with a three-valued outcome (True/False/Unknown→undecidable), distinguishing Hard constraints (must not be violated) from Soft constraints (preferences) — HardConstraint≠Preference; constraint priority across seven categories is itself governance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Feasible action set ... \mathcal A_{feasible}(K,C) as the actions that satisfy all applicable hard constraints. Decision-making should operate primarily over \mathcal A_{feasible}. ... Decision optimization ... a^* = \arg\max_{a\in\mathcal A_{feasible}} EU(a\mid K) is a standard decision-theoretic f
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the feasible action set A_feasible(K,C) (hard-constraint-satisfying actions) over which a*=argmax EU(a|K) is computed, valid only when utility/probability/constraints are all well-defined.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Multi-objective decision ... U(a)=(U_1(a),U_2(a),...,U_n(a)). Cost, Availability, Security, Time. There may be no single naturally correct scalarization. ... Pareto optimality ... \mathcal A_{Pareto} contains non-dominated actions. This is often better than inventing arbitrary weights. ... Example .
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a multi-objective utility vector and Pareto-optimal action set A_Pareto (non-dominated actions), worked with a three-action Cost/Risk/Downtime example showing no universally best action — organizational preference decides.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision policy ... DecisionPolicy specifies how alternatives are evaluated. objective priorities; risk tolerance; minimum evidence; approval requirements; acceptable uncertainty; tie-breaking rules. ... Decision policy is governance ... EU(a_1)>EU(a_2). But whether the organization is allowed to se
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines DecisionPolicy (priorities/tolerance/minimum-evidence/approval requirements/tie-breaking) and states Optimization ≠ Authorization: mathematically superior does not mean organizationally permitted.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Human decision ... KnowledgeOS may produce DecisionRecommendation rather than Decision. Parallel migration has the strongest risk-adjusted profile, but Architecture Board approval is required. This is a much safer architecture. ... Decision authority ... Authority(D,Role,Ctx) and DecisionPermission(
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires KnowledgeOS produce DecisionRecommendation, not Decision, when human authority is required — Recommended ≠ Authorized.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi's role ... Sārathi is not "the AI that decides everything." Sārathi = Decision Support and Decision Governance Orchestrator. It takes K,\Delta,G,\mathcal A,C,Risk,Policy and produces DecisionRecommendation. Where authorized, it may produce Decision. ... Lord's role ... Lord: (K,\Delta,G) \ri
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Sārathi as Decision Support and Decision Governance Orchestrator (K,Δ,G,A,C,Risk,Policy→DecisionRecommendation, or Decision when authorized), refining the clean triad Zero=Discrepancy, Lord=Possibility, Sārathi=Decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Goal → discrepancy → action ... Goal \rightarrow IdealState \rightarrow Discrepancy \rightarrow CandidateActions \rightarrow Decision \rightarrow Action. This is a core KnowledgeOS transformation chain.
b_rows_sample.statement: Assembles the core transformation chain Goal→IdealState→Discrepancy→CandidateActions→Decision→Action.

a_aliases: Action, Intervention, Control, Risk and Feedback
b_aliases: Step 21: Goals, Intentions, Decisions, Actions, Utility, Risk, Constraints, and Outcomes

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'action-intervention-control-risk-algebra' POSSIBLY relates to 'goals-decisions-actions-utility-risk-outcomes' (batch B0022). Note: S0918's Step 25Z: the pivot from epistemology to action, formalizing intervention, action contracts, risk/reversibility/blast-radius, and a safe LLM-to-execution architecture; extends B0021's goals-decisions-actions-utility-risk-outcomes (S0878/Step 21) with proof-obligation-gated preconditions and the reinterpreted Zero-at-the-action-boundary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: AAG=(V,E) ... V=V_C∪V_K∪V_I∪V_E∪V_T∪V_F
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the Architecture Assurance Graph AAG=(V,E) with node types V_C (components/bounded contexts), V_K (contracts), V_I (invariants), V_E (enforcement mechanisms), V_T (verification tests), V_F (evidence/artifacts), and typed edges Component-owns->Invariant, Contract-carries->SemanticProperty, Mechanism-enforces->Invariant, Test-verifies->Invariant, Evidence-supports->Test/Claim.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I -> Owner -> Mechanism -> Test -> Evidence
a_rows_sample.statement: For a critical property I, the complete assurance chain is I->Owner->Mechanism->Test->Evidence; a missing edge is potentially an assurance gap. Worked example: I_Authority->Governance->AuthorizationPolicy->NegativeTest->TestEvidence is a complete chain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A — Defined and enforced ... D — Claimed but unverifiable
a_rows_sample.statement: Every invariant is classified into one of four situations: (A) defined and enforced and verified; (B) defined but not enforced (M=empty); (C) implemented but not architecturally declared (a mechanism exists but nobody established which invariant it protects); (D) claimed but unverifiable (documentation asserts I=True but no evidence exists). D is flagged as particularly dangerous.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Gap(I)=RequiredAssurance(I)-ActualAssurance(I) ... Gap(I) in {None,Low,Medium,High,Critical}
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines assurance gap conceptually as Gap(I)=RequiredAssurance(I)-ActualAssurance(I), explicitly refusing to assign arbitrary numerical values and instead classifying into {None,Low,Medium,High,Critical} 'until we establish a justified scoring model'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Component correctness =/=> System correctness
a_rows_sample.statement: An architecture may have every individual bounded context (Evidence, Assessment, Governance) correct while still having a critical global assurance gap, e.g. if the contract Assessment->Governance silently drops uncertainty; boxed conclusion: component correctness does not imply system correctness.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Assurance(I_global) <= min{Assurance(I_1),Assurance(I_2),...}
a_rows_sample.statement: States a weakest-link property: for a critical end-to-end property I_global, assurance is bounded by the minimum assurance of its constituent links, explicitly qualified as 'not a universal mathematical law; it is a useful conservative assurance model' — if one indispensable boundary lacks a provenance guarantee, end-to-end provenance cannot be honestly claimed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Traceability_syntactic=True but Traceability_historical=False
a_rows_sample.statement: Decision traceability example D->A->E: traceability is only True if each reference (Decision->Assessment ID->Evidence ID) remains resolvable and semantically versioned; if the Assessment ID resolves only to the latest Assessment, syntactic traceability can hold while historical traceability fails — 'this distinction is crucial'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: SyntacticCorrectness =/= SemanticCorrectness ... HTTP 200 ... JSON schema valid
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes SyntacticCorrectness != SemanticCorrectness: an HTTP 200 proves transport success but not BusinessMeaningCorrect; a valid JSON schema does not prove SemanticContractValid.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A=(A_s,A_m,A_e,A_t,A_p,A_g)
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a candidate six-dimension KnowledgeOS assurance vector A=(A_s,A_m,A_e,A_t,A_p,A_g): A_s structural (component exists, boundary explicit, dependencies controlled, contracts defined), A_m semantic (meaning preserved, no overloaded concept, no Boolean replacing a richer state), A_e epistemic/statistical (evidence, inference, assumptions, uncertainty, correlation vs causation, model version), A_t temporal (which version/policy/model applied when, historical reconstructability), A_p provenance (claim origin, traversable chain), A_g governance (who was authorized, under which valid policy, permission vs execution).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Vector assurance is preferable to premature scalarization
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues a single global assurance score is dangerous: if A_s=1 but A_p=0, a scalar like 0.83 could falsely imply reasonable assurance, whereas for critical systems one missing indispensable property may be enough to block certification; boxed principle: vector assurance is preferable to premature scalarization — an explicit statistical-design principle.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C0 — Informational ... C4 — Critical assurance
a_rows_sample.statement: Provisionally classifies invariant criticality into five levels: C0 Informational (documentation/style), C1 Functional (normal business behavior), C2 Semantic (meaning/context preservation), C3 Governance (authority/policy/compliance), C4 Critical assurance (safety, irreversible action, high-impact decision, legally significant state); flagged as needing later validation against real KnowledgeOS use cases.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Mechanism(I)=f(Criticality(I))
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes assurance-mechanism selection as a function of criticality: low-risk -> Documentation+UnitTest; medium -> IntegrationTest+ContractTest; high -> PropertyBasedTest+Replay+AuditEvidence; critical -> FormalModel/Proof where practical — self-labeled 'a proposed framework, not yet a frozen standard'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A=(InputRef,ModelRef,InstructionRef,Output,Uncertainty,Validation,Provenance)
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an AI-generated-artifact metadata schema A=(InputRef,ModelRef,InstructionRef,Output,Uncertainty,Validation,Provenance), stating the schema must be derived from the actual KnowledgeOS implementation but conceptually AI output should not be treated as an unexplained opaque fact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: AI -> CandidateResult -> DeterministicValidation -> AcceptedArtifact. Not: AI -> ProductionTruth
a_rows_sample.statement: States the architecture must route AI output through AI->CandidateResult->DeterministicValidation->AcceptedArtifact, never directly AI->ProductionTruth, calling this distinction 'central to our KnowledgeOS design'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: TrustedFor(x,p,t) ... Valid(x,Context,Time,Purpose)
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against another bare Boolean (`trusted = true`); trust/assurance must be contextual, TrustedFor(x,p,t) — an artifact trustworthy for Task_1 need not be trustworthy for Task_2. Generalizes to Valid(x) being usually incomplete; the better form is Valid(x,Context,Time,Purpose), called 'a major insight for KnowledgeOS': validity is not absolute but ValidForPurpose(P).

a_rows_sample.anchor: StructuralValid ... SemanticValid ... EpistemicallyValid ... TemporallyValid ... GovernanceValid
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes five validity types (Structural/Semantic/Epistemic/Temporal/Governance Valid), concluding Valid(x) should be treated as shorthand only when the intended dimension is explicitly known.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Different missing edges represent different classes of architectural weakness
a_rows_sample.statement: States the missing-node principle: Invariant->Owner with no Enforcement is a design gap; Enforcement->Test missing is an assurance gap; Test->Evidence missing is an auditability gap — different missing edges are different classes of architectural weakness, letting the architecture 'diagnose itself' via forall I_i: Complete(AAG(I_i))? producing a reproducible gap report.

a_rows_sample.anchor: System -> Output + EvidenceOfCorrectness
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the architecture's strongest form as System->Output+EvidenceOfCorrectness rather than merely System->Output, stated as precisely what deterministic assurance is trying to accomplish.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We should not claim: 'The architecture is mathematically proven.' ... FormalizableArchitecture
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit self-warning: the architecture must not be claimed as mathematically proven; what exists is a FormalizableArchitecture, and the next task is determining which portions can actually be Formalized->Specified->Verified.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ### DDD ... VERY STRONG ... Gītā 1–4 ... DEEP CONSISTENCY
a_rows_sample.statement: Step 211 verdict: DDD, Mathematics, Statistics, Governance, and AI are each rated VERY STRONG, and Gita chapters 1-4 rated DEEP CONSISTENCY, citing continued distinctions Identity!=State, Knowledge!=Action, Capability!=Authority, PastState!=CurrentState, Decision!=Outcome.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The most damaging collision is E-binding #2 vs #5, which occurs INSIDE ONE FILE (Step 210)
b_rows_sample.statement: Of the twelve distinct bindings of the glyph E catalogued across the band, the most damaging collision is internal to a single file: Step 210 Section 210.20 writes E_1⇒P (an evidence item entailing a proposition), and Step 210 Section 210.30, ten sections later, writes E_1=documentation (the weakest rung of an assurance ladder) -- same symbol, same file, incompatible types, no disambiguation, no notice.

b_rows_sample.statement: Inventory of new identifier families minted across Steps 208-215: I_L/I_C/I_S (3), I_KOS members (8), P_1-P_4 (4), L_1-L_2 (2), I1-I15 (15, reprinted in 212), E_1-E_5 v1 (5), A_s..A_g (6), C0-C4 (5), situations A-D (4), AuthorityLevel states (5), E_0-E_5 v2 recalibrated (6), G1-G5 (5), G-01-G-15 (15), Status(I) values (5), Gap(I) v1 (5), Gap(I) v2 different set (5), F/D/P/U (4), E_1-E_5 primary/secondary split (2), KState values (8), ELG edge types (7), 14-code type taxonomy (14), Epoch_1-Epoch_5 (5), architecture senses (4) -- totalling 162 new identifiers minted in this 8-file band, excluding one-off symbols.

b_rows_sample.statement: The band's 162 new identifiers collide at the glyph level with at least five prior corpus invariant-naming families with zero acknowledgement: I1-I20 (prior) vs I1-I15 (Step 210/212) is a direct namespace collision with different meanings and no disambiguation; INV-1-INV-20 occupies the same conceptual space as I1-I15/I_KOS with disjoint naming; C1-C7 (prior) directly collides with C0-C4 (Step 211 criticality) and also with Step 208's contracts C_1/C_2/C_3, Step 209's contexts C, and Step 214's claims C_1/C_2 -- five bindings of C_n in the band plus the prior family; AFR-01-AFR-36 and G-01-G-15 are two parallel audit/fitness registers unaware of each other; GT/GG/GE/GC/GA collides conceptually with G1-G5, G-01-G-15, G_P, and G_i (six bindings of G total, including the Governance bounded context itself); S1-S6 collides with seven in-band bindings of S; K1-K7 collides with KState, K_t, and V_K; V1-V10 collides with V_i, the vertex set V, and the six V_C/V_K/V_I/V_E/V_T/V_F node classes. Under LATER != SUPERSEDING, none of the prior families is superseded -- the corpus now carries two or more parallel, mutually unaware invariant registries over the same architecture. Families IR/CM/LA/AAI/PLP are not mentioned, reconciled, or superseded at all.

a_rows_sample.statement: D-1: Phase A's high-confidence Observed claim of 8 wired hooks is wrong; the actual count via a JSON-parsing method is 10 (PreToolUse 5, PostToolUse 2, SessionStart 1, Stop 2), the original figure having been eyeballed rather than computed, with settings.json unchanged since the baseline commit ruling out temporal drift.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t is the smallest possible unit of knowledge about an observation at time t.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes, and repeatedly re-affirms as a 'candidate definition, not yet formally proven', K_t(o) = the smallest epistemically meaningful unit of knowledge about observation o at time t, explicitly warning against prematurely identifying K_t with a data point, a claim, or the existing six-tuple (entity/property/context/relation/time/authority) -- those may become representations of K_t, not K_t itself, restated as the invariant 'Representation != Knowledge Identity'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can K_t be decomposed into smaller knowledge units without losing the knowledge about the observation? If yes, it wasn't minimal. If no, we have a candidate minimal knowledge unit.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes an operational minimality criterion for K_t via a decomposition test (K_t -> {K_t,1, K_t,2, ...}): if the decomposition preserves all knowledge about the observation, the original unit was not minimal; if no such decomposition exists, it is a candidate minimal unit -- offered as a way to formalize 'smallest' without prematurely fixing K_t's internal structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A sentence is a linguistic representation that may contain one or more K_t units. ... the number of sentences gives us a possible dimensional view, but not necessarily the true number of dimensions.
a_rows_sample.statement: Using a repeated Nexus-server worked example (RHEL 9.8, 8 vCPU, port 8081, etc. as ten atomic statements), argues a sentence is not necessarily one K_t unit -- e.g. 'has 8 vCPUs and 31 GB RAM' contains two atomic units -- and that an observation's true dimensionality is not bounded by however many sentences currently describe it (K_t(O) subset-of all potentially observable aspects of O; 'Knowledge at t != the complete observation'); new sentences discovered later add new dimensions (K_t^11), and a corrected statement changes an existing dimension's value rather than necessarily creating a new one.

a_rows_sample.anchor: WorldState_t -> Observation_t^A -> InformationState_t^A -> EpistemicState_t^A -> KnowledgeAttribution, with history H_{<=t} preserved. It then proposes K_t^{A,R} as a time-indexed knowledge attribution, dependent on participant A, extraction regime R.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reading an unread-in-this-batch corpus document, reports its chain WorldState_t -> Observation_t^A -> InformationState_t^A -> EpistemicState_t^A -> KnowledgeAttribution (with preserved history H_{<=t}) and its participant/regime-relative K_t^{A,R}; explicitly distinguishes this from the dialogue's own new atomic-K_t hypothesis, treating the latter as a possible FURTHER refinement (one measurable statement per observation dimension) rather than something the attached document already established, and notes the document's own probability treatment P(K_t^A|F_t^A) as extraction-uncertainty, explicitly distinct from Knowledge itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q = domain of possible items; K subset-of Q = a particular knowledge state; script-K = space/family of possible states; probability (Q, script-K, p). The crucial distinction is: script-K != K_t != P(K_t | O_{<=t}).
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports a Knowledge Space Theory (KST) formalism (Q as domain of possible items, K as a particular state, script-K as the family of possible states, with probability attached as (Q,script-K,p)) as external confirmation that a knowledge-space, a particular state, and a probability distribution over states are three genuinely different objects; notes KST's own K_t is a learner-capability state (a different, narrower sense than the dialogue's broader KnowledgeOS K_t), and that the dialogue's atomic-unit idea asks a question KST does not answer: what is the state/value of each individual knowledge unit within a state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(k_i | E) is the epistemic confidence/degree of support for proposition k_i, given the available evidence. ... k_i != P(k_i)
a_rows_sample.statement: Repeatedly insists that probability attached to a knowledge unit must be given a precise referent -- distinguishing P(claim is true), P(claim is supported by available evidence), P(the measurement/extraction is correct), and P(claim belongs to K_t) as not necessarily the same quantity, and stating k_i != P(k_i): the knowledge unit itself is not identical to its probability. Also proposes that not every claim's epistemic measure need be a probability -- it could be categorical status, an interval, a confidence level, measurement uncertainty, or logical entailment strength -- warning against forcing every kind of knowledge into probability merely because probability is mathematically convenient.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Observation -> Atomic propositions -> Evidence -> Measured epistemic state -> Ideal/reference state -> distance -> knowledge gap. This potentially connects several previously separate strands: Phase 1 ... Phase 2 ... KST ... Pritchard ... Zero ... Knower ... Evidence ... Kernel
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a 'candidate unifying structure, not yet a completed theory': Observation -> Atomic propositions -> Evidence -> Measured epistemic state -> Ideal/reference state -> distance -> knowledge gap, claimed to potentially connect the corpus's Phase-1 (knowledge as relationship/justification/state evolution), Phase-2 (Knowledge Space/participant/time/projection), KST (Q, script-K, K_t, p), Pritchard's belief-counts-as-knowledge conditions, Zero, Knower-ownership, Evidence/determination, and Kernel-as-substrate strands, while explicitly warning against collapsing these prematurely.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EpistemicState = Acquisition x Support x Resolution x Validity
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports a multidimensional EpistemicState formulation (Acquisition x Support x Resolution x Validity) as already-derived corpus material supporting the general direction of a non-monolithic, multi-axis knowledge state, alongside a stated distinction chain Knowledge!=Reality, Observation!=Knowledge, Dimension!=Statement, Dimension!=Value, Guidance!=Decision, Zero!=Knowledge, Parsing!=Knowledge, Parsing!=Dimension-Discovery.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What is the minimum structure of k_t such that the entire KnowledgeOS theory — evidence, probability, context, identity, Zero, evolution, proposal, decision and action — can be derived without adding arbitrary architectural assumptions?
a_rows_sample.statement: Closes the file's line of inquiry with an explicit unresolved research question: what is the minimal structure of the atomic knowledge unit k_t from which the rest of the theory (evidence, probability, context, identity, Zero, evolution, proposal, decision, action) could be derived without arbitrary additional architectural assumptions -- stated as the next major research question rather than answered.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A sentence is not automatically a knowledge dimension merely because it is syntactically a sentence. ... independent knowledge-bearing statement -> candidate dimension
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates the minimal-knowledge-unit hypothesis k_t(O) (smallest independently meaningful unit of knowledge about an observation at t) with the qualification that sentence != dimension automatically -- semantic independence of a statement must be established before it counts as a candidate dimension; and states K_t(O) is necessarily partial, since K_t(O) subset-of D(O), the full (possibly unbounded) dimension set of the observation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: k_i = (O, d_i, v_i, t, E_i, p_i, q_i)
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the atomic knowledge claim to a seven-field tuple k_i=(O,d_i,v_i,t,E_i,p_i,q_i) -- observation, semantic dimension, claimed value, time, evidence/information source, epistemic probability, and an explicit information-sufficiency/support status q_i -- with K_t(O)={k_1,...,k_n} as the resulting knowledge state, and reiterates that dimensionality is representation-relative rather than an intrinsic finite property of the object (a sentence maps to one or more atomic claims, not one-to-one).

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t should not be identified with a Kripke model or possible-world set. Status: research conclusion / compatibility constraint, not yet kernel theorem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Confirms the DEL document's rejection of K_t as a Kripke pointed model (M,w) strengthens (without proving) the corpus's independently-developed atomic-tuple direction k_i=(O,d_i,v_i,t,E_i,C_i,p_i,q_i); explicitly records the possible-worlds rejection as a research conclusion/compatibility constraint, not a kernel theorem.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The missing step is: $$(O,E_{\le t},A,G,EC)\;\longrightarrow\;K_t(O)$$ ... The file itself almost explicitly states this as the unanswered operation \(\mathcal M\): $$\mathcal M:(O,E_{\le t},A,G,EC)\rightarrow K_t(O)$$
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the central missing derivation in the reviewed K_t/observation research as the unanswered operation M:(O, E_{<=t}, A, G, EC) -> K_t(O) -- the document being reviewed 'repeatedly approaches it but never actually derives it' -- where O is observation, E_{<=t} is evidence up to time t, A is the Knower/agent, G is goal, and EC is the epistemic contract.

a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects/sharpens the atomic-knowledge-unit hypothesis by pointing out that reviewed prior work jumps directly from an observation O to a set of atoms k_1..k_n without deriving them, despite itself distinguishing dimension != statement != knowledge atom != value; the transformation producing the atoms from an observation is never actually supplied.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$O\overset{\mathcal D}{\longrightarrow}\{d_i\}\overset{\mathcal P}{\longrightarrow}\{q_i\}\overset{\mathcal E}{\longrightarrow}\{s_{i,t}\}\overset{\mathcal A}{\longrightarrow}K_t$$ where \(O\) = observation; \(d_i\) = observable/aspect dimension; \(q_i\) = atomic proposition ...; \(s_{i,t}\) = epistemic state/value ...; \(K_t\) = resulting knowledge state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes decomposing the missing K_t-construction derivation into a four-operator pipeline: D (observation to dimensions {d_i}), P (dimensions to atomic propositions {q_i}), E (propositions to epistemic-state values {s_i,t}), and A (values aggregated to K_t) -- named as the candidate missing derivation, with a worked Nexus-server example (RHEL 9.8, 8 vCPU, 31GB RAM, port 8081, etc. -> candidate atoms k_i) illustrating that no mathematical operation currently justifies which atoms are 'correct'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$K_t=\operatorname{Aggregate}(k_{1,t},\ldots,k_{n,t})$$ and we must determine whether that aggregation is: a set, vector, graph, distribution, state space, or something else. That is explicitly still open in the document.
a_rows_sample.statement: Names a second missing derivation: the aggregation of individual knowledge atoms {k_i,t} into the knowledge state K_t, with the mathematical type of the aggregate (set/vector/graph/distribution/state-space/other) left explicitly open.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I think the previous research was looking for the missing piece **one level too late**. We kept asking: What is \(D(K_t,I_t)\)? But before that, we need: How is \(K_t\) generated? And before that: How is an observation transformed into atomic knowledge propositions?
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues the research programme has been searching for the missing piece at the wrong level: the priority order of open questions should be (1) how is an observation transformed into atomic knowledge propositions, before (2) how is K_t generated from those atoms, before (3) what is the comparison function D(K_t,I_t) -- reordering research priority away from the distance function toward the earlier construction steps.

a_rows_sample.anchor: $$R_t\overset{\operatorname{Obs}_A}{\longrightarrow}O_t^A$$ where \(R_t\) is the world/reality state and \(O_t^A\) is what participant \(A\) can observe. ... consistent with the document's existing ... projection $$\Pi_A:\mathcal W\rightarrow\mathcal E_A$$ but the document explicitly treats that projection as a hypothesis rather than an established theory.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies an even deeper missing derivation than K_t-construction: the theory currently starts with observation O as given, but a genuinely epistemological theory must also derive Reality -> Observation, i.e. R_t --Obs_A--> O_t^A (world/reality state to what a specific participant A can observe), consistent with but more explicit than the document's existing (hypothesis-only) projection Pi_A: W -> E_A.

a_rows_sample.anchor: **The Knowledge-State Construction Derivation** $$R_t\rightarrow O_t^A\rightarrow Q_t^A\rightarrow E_t^A\rightarrow K_t^A$$ followed by: $$(A,G,EC)\rightarrow I_t^A\rightarrow Z_t^A\rightarrow\text{investigation/action}\rightarrow K_{t+1}^A$$ ... it has not derived the **transformations between the nodes**.
a_rows_sample.statement: Names and consolidates the overall missing derivation as 'The Knowledge-State Construction Derivation': R_t -> O_t^A -> Q_t^A -> E_t^A -> K_t^A, followed by (A,G,EC) -> I_t^A -> Z_t^A -> investigation/action -> K_{t+1}^A; concludes the prior work has developed almost all the nodes of this pipeline but never derived the transformations connecting them, and that the most important missing function is the decomposition of M:(O,E_{<=t},A,G,EC) -> K_t into formally justified sub-operations.

b_rows_sample.anchor: k_i = (q_i, v_i, p_i, E_i, t_i, A_i)
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the atomic knowledge unit into an explicit six-field tuple k_i=(q_i,v_i,p_i,E_i,t_i,A_i): question/proposition, observed value, epistemic measurement, evidence, temporal validity, and authority/provenance -- explicitly not a bare sentence and not a bare scalar probability, motivated by Knowledge Space Theory's separation of a latent state from an estimated/assessed state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: script-K != K_t != hat-K_t ... K — Knowledge Space ... K_t — Actual knowledge state ... hat-K_t — measured/extracted knowledge state
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes three objects with KnowledgeOS-specific interpretation: script-K (Knowledge Space, all admissible knowledge states about a domain/observation), K_t (the actual/latent underlying epistemic state), and hat-K_t (what KnowledgeOS currently infers/measures from available evidence) -- directly supported by KST's latent-state/assessment distinction, and offered as one of the strongest mathematical contributions obtained so far.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Epistemic uncertainty: U_t(q_i)=f(p_i) ... State discrepancy: D_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t) ... These are not the same thing.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes two genuinely different gaps that had previously been conflated: epistemic uncertainty U_t(q_i)=f(p_i) (how certain we are that a given measurement is correct) versus state discrepancy D_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t) (how far the measured state is from the ideal/required state); illustrated by two contrasting cases -- high confidence (p=0.999) with a large discrepancy (meaning we are highly certain the system is wrong) versus moderate confidence (p=0.55) with unknown discrepancy (meaning we don't know whether the system is wrong).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Z_t=0 does not automatically mean Truth=1, because our measurement itself may be uncertain. That preserves the earlier distinction between confidence and authority.
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines Zero(K_t,I_t,E_t) as a distance evaluation Z_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t) with Z_t=0 meaning hat-K_t is equivalent to I_t under the dimensions/metric being evaluated, but explicitly warns Z_t=0 does not thereby entail Truth=1, since the measurement producing hat-K_t may itself be uncertain -- preserving the confidence-vs-authority distinction.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Case A — knowledge changes, observation does not ... Case B — observation changes ... Case C — both
b_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the previously repeatedly-raised open question ('does a changed knowledge state mean a changed observation?') into three explicit cases: Case A, O_t=O_{t+1} but K_t!=K_{t+1} (a new dimension was discovered or better evidence obtained, the object itself did not change); Case B, O_t!=O_{t+1} (the actual observed entity changed); Case C, both change simultaneously -- giving a proper temporal model for the identity question the corpus had left explicitly unresolved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS = KST-compatible state mathematics + epistemic semantics + temporal semantics + provenance + governance
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly lists what Knowledge Space Theory does NOT solve for KnowledgeOS (truth, provenance, authority, justification, historical reconstruction, observation identity, institutional knowledge, contextual knowledge, non-monotonic revision, the meaning of an Ideal State, the atomic-knowledge-unit notion itself), rejecting the identification KnowledgeOS=KST in favor of KnowledgeOS = KST-compatible state mathematics + epistemic semantics + temporal semantics + provenance + governance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: G1 — Atomic Knowledge ... G2 — State space ... G3 — Probability ... G4 — Ideal State ... G5 — Distance ... G6 — Dynamics
b_rows_sample.statement: Reduces the theory's open problems from ten to six named research gaps: G1 precisely defining k_i and its atomicity criterion; G2 defining script-K's mathematical structure (set system? lattice? measurable space? something richer?); G3 defining P(k_i|E_<=t) precisely, distinguishing uncertainty from truth and authority; G4 mathematically defining the Ideal State I_t(O,C,G), called probably the most important remaining gap; G5 defining the distance function Delta_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t), possibly non-Euclidean; G6 defining the transition K_t->K_{t+1} and typing what kind of change (new information, correction, discovery, revision, observation change, or identity change) it represents.

b_rows_sample.anchor: k_i = (O, d_i, v_i, t, E_i, C_i, q_i, rho_i) where rho_i is not necessarily a scalar probability.
b_rows_sample.statement: Revises the atomic knowledge tuple to replace the scalar probability field with rho_i (not necessarily scalar), with probabilistic support instead represented externally through the joint conditional model Pi_t=L(X|F_t), from which p_i=Pi_t(X_i=v_i) is a derived query; also proposes an alternative five-component Knowledge State K_t(O)=(claims C_t, evidence/provenance E_t, determinations D_t, relations/dependencies R_t, contextual state X_t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: c=(O,d,A,t) ... kappa(c)=(E,C,q,status,provenance,...) ... probabilistic information is not stored inside the semantic claim as its essence.
b_rows_sample.statement: Splits the knowledge-claim tuple into a semantic core c=(O,d,A,t) (object, dimension, measurable proposition, temporal reference) and separate epistemic metadata kappa(c)=(E,C,q,status,provenance,...), with probability computed on top as P_t(A)=P(A|F_t) rather than embedded as the claim's essence -- refining the earlier atomic-tuple candidates from prior files in this same research line.

Note: Building on Knowledge Space Theory's latent-vs-estimated-state distinction, proposes a six-field atomic knowledge unit k_i=(q_i,v_i,p_i,E_i,t_i,A_i) (question/proposition, observed value, epistemic measurement/probability, evidence, temporal validity, authority/provenance) rather than a bare sentence or scalar; a three-way state distinction script-K (Knowledge Space, all admissible states) != K_t (actual/latent state) != hat-K_t (measured/extracted state); a critical distinction between epistemic uncertainty U_t(q_i)=f(p_i) (how certain is the measurement) and state discrepancy D_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t) (how far the measured state is from the ideal state) -- explicitly not the same thing, illustrated by cases of high confidence in a wrong measurement (p=0.999, D=large) versus low confidence with unknown discrepancy (p=0.55, D=unknown); a three-case temporal-identity resolution (Case A: knowledge changes, observation doesn't; Case B: observation changes; Case C: both) answering a previously-unresolved question; a generalized KnowledgeOS-specific Knowledge Space script-K(O,C,R) (admissible epistemic states for observation O under context C and regime R, distinguished from KST's own (Q,script-K)); an explicit list of what KST does NOT solve (truth, provenance, authority, justification, historical reconstruction, observation identity, institutional/contextual knowledge, non-monotonic revision, Ideal State meaning, the atomic-unit notion itself); and a reduction of the theory's open problems from ten to six named gaps G1 (atomic knowledge k_i), G2 (state space script-K's mathematical structure), G3 (probability semantics), G4 (Ideal State formalization, called probably the most important remaining gap), G5 (distance function, possibly non-Euclidean), G6 (dynamics/transition typing).

a_rows_sample.anchor: It is a NORMATIVE DECISION, not a mathematical result. Nothing in the model FORCES authority to be exogenous ... Step 187 §187.23's own B ... is exactly the recorded artefact that re-enters the cycle. The stipulation cuts the edge in the ARCHITECTURE while B keeps it in the REPRESENTATION.
a_rows_sample.statement: Finding ON-1: the corpus does break the 7-node cycle via Step 187's stipulation that authority is exogenous (Authority subset Actor x Action x Context x Time, with no Assertion in it), but this is classified as a normative decision, not a mathematical result -- the theory is acyclic if and only if authority is exogenous, and that exogeneity is declared rather than derived, making every theorem about K conditional on an unspecified external authority oracle; moreover Step 187's own field B (the recorded normative/provenance basis of an authority state) is exactly the artefact that re-enters the cycle at the representational level, so semantic closure and governance closure are not both achieved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the constitutional layer is a NORMATIVE DECISION with an architectural justification, not a mathematical result. The corpus does not say this; it presents §187.29 as a finding. ... every theorem about K is then conditional on an EXTERNAL AUTHORITY ORACLE whose behaviour the theory never specifies.
a_rows_sample.statement: Finding GR-3: directly answers the mandate's four-way classification question -- the constitutional layer (authority as exogenous) is NOT mathematically necessary (a self-referential/fixed-point authority model is consistent, merely harder), IS architecturally necessary (without it the dependency graph is cyclic, per 03-FOUNDATIONAL-ONTOLOGY.md ON-1), is empirically only partially observed and the observation cuts against the stipulation (see GR-4/GR-5), and is fundamentally NORMATIVE -- Step 187 decides authority is exogenous and presents that decision as a finding rather than labelling it as a decision; every theorem about K is therefore conditional on an unspecified external authority oracle, consistent with Step 266 listing Authority as class C.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge is always knowledge-at-a-time within an evolving Knowledge Space.
a_rows_sample.statement: C-15 (a formal Kernel candidate about retraction) is reframed: rather than 'Knowledge can be retracted', the deeper model is 'Knowledge is always knowledge-at-a-time within an evolving Knowledge Space.' A projection is a view/selection of the evolving space at a point in time per perspective/purpose/agent/context; 'Knowledge X was true/justified at T1' does not necessarily imply 'X must remain true/usable at T2' — historical knowledge doesn't disappear, a later projection simply doesn't contain it as currently applicable.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We must **not now conclude that Projection solves C-15**. That would be jumping from brainstorming into architecture.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit governance discipline: the brainstorming Projection idea must not be treated as solving C-15, only as an alternative hypothesis — 'Maybe temporal change belongs to the relationship between Knowledge Space and Projection rather than to the epistemic state of the Knowledge object itself' — which C-15 should test, not adopt directly.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ### KnowledgeCore ... ### Projection ... ### Knowledge Space ... ### Kernel
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposed four-part separation: KnowledgeCore protects identity, justification, admissibility, epistemic history, continuity; Projection answers 'what knowledge is relevant/visible/applicable from this perspective at this time?'; Knowledge Space represents the broader evolving space in which knowledge exists and changes; Kernel protects the fundamental epistemic guarantees without becoming the entire cognitive system. Illustrated with an AI system example: 09:00 projection 'customer is eligible' vs 14:00 projection 'customer is not currently eligible' after new evidence, without erasing the 09:00 knowledge — described as closer to a 'persistent epistemic brain' than a simple CRUD knowledge base.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Absence must not silently become an epistemic state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Danger flagged in the Projection model: 'If Projection P2 doesn't contain X, therefore X is false' would be wrong, since absence from a projection could mean not relevant, not visible, not assessed, outside scope, unavailable, superseded, or genuinely no longer justified — these are different meanings. This connects to the ZERO lens: absence must not silently become an epistemic state, giving another reason to preserve ZERO discipline within the Projection idea.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The formal Kernel work is deliberately asking: **What is the smallest authoritative boundary?** Your brainstorming was asking a different question: **What kind of epistemic world would make such a Kernel useful?**
a_rows_sample.statement: Two complementary but distinct questions must not be mixed during adjudication: the formal Kernel work asks 'What is the smallest authoritative boundary?' while the brainstorming asks 'What kind of epistemic world would make such a Kernel useful?' Recommended sequence: BRAINSTORMING (Knowledge/Knowledge Space/Time/Projection/Identity/Evidence/Reasoning) -> FORMAL KERNEL (what must absolutely be protected) -> ADJUDICATION (what is actually constitutional) -> FALSIFICATION (can the broader model break the proposed minimal Kernel) -> FUTURE ARCHITECTURE -> FUTURE VISION ('brain' of an AI/computer system).

a_rows_sample.anchor: | Brainstorming hypothesis | Current law | Potential challenge |
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes producing three artifacts: (A) Current Law — what KnowledgeOS currently constitutionally says; (B) Brainstorming Conceptual Model — what has been imagined/researched as possible models; (C) Falsification Matrix — where B challenges A. Gives a worked six-row example table (e.g. 'Knowledge is time-dependent' vs 'History is forward-only' -> 'Does time belong to state or projection?'; 'Knowledge can disappear from a projection without becoming false' vs 'ZERO' -> 'Strong compatibility').

a_rows_sample.anchor: Retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status.
a_rows_sample.statement: Evaluating a prior (unnamed) review's proposal: 'Retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status' is assessed as a genuinely important, strong hypothesis — represented as Epistemic condition (e.g. VERIFIED) staying constant while a separate Lifecycle (e.g. ACTIVE -> RETRACTED) changes, rather than an epistemic-state transition VERIFIED->RETRACTED. This protects the distinction 'currently relied upon' != 'true' — 'we no longer rely on X' does not mean 'X is false' — assessed as one of the strongest points in the review.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "Lifecycle status already exists" is not established... It proposes four lifecycle states — that's already architecture
a_rows_sample.statement: Challenges the prior review on two counts: (1) its claim 'the Kernel already supports lifecycle transitions' is not established without checking v1.1 — a forward-only lifecycle existing is a different proposition from a separate lifecycle-state-model existing; (2) proposing four lifecycle states (PROPOSED/ACTIVE/RETRACTED/SUPERSEDED) from the orthogonality finding alone is 'architecture by inference' — the Zero lens can show retraction need not be an epistemic state, but cannot by itself justify a specific four-state machine. Separates Finding ('retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status') from Hypothesis ('a lifecycle axis could represent that orthogonality') from Proposed architecture ('Kernel contains a four-state lifecycle model') — only the first is currently a useful finding.

a_rows_sample.anchor: who is allowed to assert the retraction? That takes us directly into: **authority, agency and decision power.**
a_rows_sample.statement: C-15 may not be merely a state-model problem but a boundary-ownership problem: when 'the organization no longer relies on K123', who decides that — KnowledgeCore, Authority, Projection, Decision Boundary, an external business context, or a governance process — and who is allowed to assert the retraction? This is an open question connecting directly to authority, agency, and decision power.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can the lifecycle interpretation represent retraction without introducing a second hidden epistemic state machine?
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that Epistemic State + Lifecycle State could become excellent architecture or could explode into Epistemic State Machine x Lifecycle State Machine x Authority State Machine x Projection State Machine, at which point 'the small Kernel has exploded' — the ZERO lens should attack the lifecycle proposal too. Final verdict: classify the reviewed proposal as a HIGH-VALUE RESEARCH HYPOTHESIS (labeled C-15-H1: 'Retraction may be orthogonal to epistemic status and representable as lifecycle/process semantics without adding an epistemic state'), not a C-15 ruling and not an implementation instruction, to be tested against v1.1, Knowledge Space model, Projection model, Identity invariant, forward-only lifecycle, History, Agency, Authority, ZERO lens, and the minimal-boundary criterion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Vocabulary collision — flagged, unresolved. `024119` leads the projection count (49) but uses "projection" in the **CQRS read-model** sense, not the epistemic sense.
a_rows_sample.statement: The C-15-relevant material splits across two corpus regions: Retraction/withdrawal is concentrated in the early/ORIGINAL region (114358, 233040, 111647, 113410, 123619), while Projection is concentrated in the late/extraction era (110525, 140251, 135642, 155035); Temporal spans both. a_rows_sample.anchor: Session 1 should be the **research/extraction track**. Session 2 should remain the **formal adjudication track**. ... the two streams should **not contaminate each other**.
a_rows_sample.statement: Establishes a two-track separation: Session 1 (brainstorming corpus -> document-by-document extraction -> Knowledge -> Knowledge Space -> KnowledgeOS -> Kernel concepts -> research synthesis) versus Session 2 (current Kernel law -> F-CM/C-items -> falsification -> adjudication -> rulings), which must not contaminate each other; explicitly freezes Session 2 (including C-15 refinement) until the research extraction catches up. Six-layer target: (1) what did we originally think (Phase 1), (2) what did research introduce (Phase 2), (3) what contradictions appeared, (4) what concepts survived both phases, (5) what remains genuinely unresolved, (6) only then — what, if anything, belongs in the KnowledgeOS Kernel (the output of the exercise, not its starting assumption).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Now we can ask whether **retraction is actually a lifecycle concern**, or whether it is better understood as a consequence of temporal epistemic evolution. But **we should not decide that yet**.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects the Knowledge extraction's Knowledge-Space/participant/information-at-t/projection/knowledge-at-t/later-information/revision-contraction-supersession pipeline to C-15: raises whether retraction is actually a lifecycle concern or better understood as a consequence of temporal epistemic evolution, explicitly deferring the decision — exactly why extracting Knowledge first, before continuing C-15 refinement, was the right call.

a_rows_sample.statement: Terminological-only collisions separated from genuine contradictions: 'projection' now has three unmergeable senses — A CQRS/read-model projection (024119, 49 hits, leads the cluster count), B epistemic projection of a Knowledge Space (110525, 140251, 135642), C a measure over (Ω,F) (181038, contested by 181719, since sense C is a formalization of B that may not be valid). a_rows_sample.statement: Provenance finding: document 171853 (S0564) attributes its Knowledge-Space + time-indexed-projection reframing of C-15 to 'your earlier conceptual model', but tested against all 13 original-region documents this is not supported — 'knowledge space' occurs 0 times, 'at time t'/'knowledge-at-time' occurs once (113645), while 'retract'/'withdraw' occurs heavily (114358:32, 111647:24, 113410:14, 123619:11, 112855:10). b_rows_sample.anchor: the entire 257-document corpus this programme reconstructs is priority-7 evidence by the project's oldest stated rule.
b_rows_sample.statement: DOC-1 (20260801-1231 §3) establishes the project's own eight-tier evidence hierarchy: (1) implementation/source code highest, (2) executable tests/enforced invariants very high, (3) persistence/durable records very high, (4) accepted ADRs/governance decisions high, (5) architecture documentation medium-high, (6) C4/diagrams medium, (7) proposals and brainstorming low, (8) historical contextual knowledge lowest — with the rule 'a documented architecture that is not implemented is not current architecture.' Applied reflexively: the entire 257-document brainstorming corpus this programme reconstructs is itself only priority-7 evidence by the project's own oldest stated rule, meaning the reconstruction's output can only ever be candidate pressure on the formal model, never a competing authority. DOC-1 §61 also excludes 'future KnowledgeOS kernel concepts' from current EKS, and §44 states historical EKS architecture and the later KnowledgeOS target architecture are not interchangeable — the corpus's oldest document already forbids the retrospective attribution this programme guards against.

b_rows_sample.anchor: **Ruled by the HPA, 2026-08-25.** ... A reclassification edits **this census** — never a document's name or location.
b_rows_sample.statement: HPA ruling (2026-08-25): classification is metadata, not filesystem — a filename carries identity/chronology/provenance only, never a category code; cluster membership is recorded in the census, not the path (a document may belong to several clusters, a path cannot express that without arbitrary choice); a reclassification edits the census, never a document's name/location; directory names express artifact function, never subject or authority; not one source document was moved. Separately ruled: renaming kernel/ to corpus/ was considered and rejected (the semantic hazard is mitigated by rule, not layout); every directory is kept but the two levels (brainstorming/ coordination vs brainstorming/kernel/ working) must differ rather than mirror, since mirroring identical trees created ambiguity about which to use.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the same process shaped both sides of the E2 ↔ D5 interface.
a_rows_sample.statement: INFO-2: the producing process of E2 also authored the D5 establishment-criteria proposal and the canonical C-10 analysis, meaning the same process shaped both sides of the E2↔D5 interface; recorded as non-blocking but as a residual for future acts to weigh.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Adopting a completeness model is not evidence of capability existence — under D5's own scheme a definition is Class C (future/architectural) evidence, which cannot establish existence by itself.
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopting a completeness/design model for a capability is explicitly distinguished from establishing that the capability exists; such adoption is Class C (future/architectural) evidence under the D5 scheme and cannot by itself establish existence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: L1 · PROTOTYPE ESTABLISHMENT ... L2 · OPERATIONAL ESTABLISHMENT ... L3 · AUTHORITATIVE ESTABLISHMENT
a_rows_sample.statement: A three-level assurance framework for capability establishment: L1 (one realized instance, a named milestone that does NOT flip existence), L2 (≥2 independent governed acts showing the outcome is owned rather than incidental — the level at which D2/existence flips), L3 (L2 plus exercised claim-authority plus a change history — the level at which the capability may carry authoritative claims).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Option A is rejected — and on evidence, not preference: the full conjunction includes E10, which requires a history that cannot exist at establishment time. Adopting it would make C-10 permanently unestablishable.
a_rows_sample.statement: The full-conjunction Option A for establishment criteria is rejected as structurally unsatisfiable, because it requires a criterion (E10, distinct reason to change / history) that by definition cannot exist at the moment of establishment.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A summary must never silently replace the governing artifact.
a_rows_sample.statement: An appended PO/ARB act resolves a divergence between a proposal's decided §4.2 text and the adoption act's own restated summary of L3, ruling the proposal's text governs; states the general principle that a summary must never silently replace the governing artifact, and closes the divergence in the same shape as the earlier Flag-O resolution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Capability existence ≠ Capability authority ≠ Operational maturity
a_rows_sample.statement: Three distinct concepts are kept apart in the settled L1/L2/L3 model: capability existence, capability authority, and operational maturity; had L3 been read as maturity-only, the exercised-authority condition (E3) would have fallen out of the model entirely.

b_rows_sample.anchor: SUBJECT Realization | Boundary | Future-Excluded ... EPISTEMIC Observed | Inferred | Proposed | Decided | Open ... PROVENANCE Governed | Ungoverned | External-corroborative ... REPRODUCIBILITY Reproducible | Non-reproducible
b_rows_sample.statement: Four orthogonal evidence dimensions are reconciled and adopted for C-10 establishment: SUBJECT (what is it about: Realization/Boundary/Future-Excluded), EPISTEMIC (how well known: Observed/Inferred/Proposed/Decided/Open), PROVENANCE (whose artifact: Governed/Ungoverned/External-corroborative), and REPRODUCIBILITY (can anyone re-derive it: Reproducible/Non-reproducible), with the note that a DECIDED claim and a Reproducible claim are not the same thing.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Option A is not merely unjustified -- it is unsatisfiable. the full conjunction E1 and ... and E10 includes E10, and E10 requires a history that cannot exist at establishment time. Adopting Option A would make C-10 PERMANENTLY UNESTABLISHABLE
b_rows_sample.statement: Impossibility proof: adopting the full conjunctive criteria set E1 through E10 as the establishment test (Option A) would make C-10 permanently unestablishable, because E10 (operational repeatability, a sustained history) structurally cannot be satisfied at a single point in time -- disposing of Option A on evidence rather than preference.

b_rows_sample.anchor: L1 PROTOTYPE ESTABLISHMENT ... L2 OPERATIONAL ESTABLISHMENT ... L3 AUTHORITATIVE ESTABLISHMENT ... Which level flips D2? recommended: L2, not L1. one instance satisfying E1/E2/E7/E8 is still compatible with an incidental outcome
b_rows_sample.statement: A three-level assurance-level model (Option C) is recommended: L1 Prototype (semantic realized once, discriminable, reconstructable), L2 Operational (repeated across >=2 acts, lifecycle transitions real), L3 Authoritative (change history exists); D2 is recommended to flip only at L2, not L1, because a single instance is still compatible with an incidental (not owned) outcome, and E6 (repeatability across >=2 acts) is what actually shows ownership.

b_rows_sample.anchor: does the acting context OWN the outcome, or does it FALL OUT of another context's mechanism? Counterfactual form: remove C-10 -- does the receipt still appear? If yes, E7 fails.
b_rows_sample.statement: Criterion E7 (Boundary discrimination) is given an explicit counterfactual satisfaction test: remove the candidate capability and ask whether the outcome still appears; if yes, the outcome falls out of another context's mechanism (as CAP-01 bootstrap and BC-7 tokenRef leakage do for C-10) and E7 fails.

b_rows_sample.anchor: eight of nine names appear NOWHERE in the estate ... The adopted criteria have no artifact in the governed record. They arrive as names only ... this is the THIRD occurrence of the same pattern in this estate
b_rows_sample.statement: D5 is registered as DECIDED (adopting the establishment-criteria model in principle) while Governance simultaneously discovers that eight of the nine criterion names (E1-E9) appear nowhere as defined content in the estate, since the commissioned Architecture analysis had not yet been delivered -- the record holds nine labels, not nine criteria, and 'a name is not a criterion' is stated as a governing discipline.

b_rows_sample.anchor: D5 STATUS: DECIDED -- framework adopted. PROVENANCE STATUS: Architecture artifact pending. ... A good model is not the same as an authorized architectural deliverable.
b_rows_sample.statement: D5-AMD1 corrects D5's status to a two-part form (framework decision adopted; provenance/Architecture-artifact status separately pending), reaffirms Option A (full conjunction) must not be assumed as the minimum sufficient combination, and keeps the commission open (Reading 2: it stands, the eventual Architecture artifact must define E1-E10) rather than closing it as complete.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels share the notation 'E1..E10'
