a_rows_sample.anchor: TemporalPrecedence(A,B)\not\Rightarrow Causation(A,B) ... temporal ordering alone is insufficient
a_rows_sample.statement: States the first theorem-like invariant: temporal precedence does not imply causation, illustrated with an upgrade-then-outage timeline that omits an intervening firewall change as an alternative cause.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sequence, Association, CausalHypothesis, CausalKnowledge ... increasing epistemic strength
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a four-level causal-knowledge hierarchy of increasing epistemic strength: Sequence (A≺B, directly observable ordering), Association (A~B, statistical association), CausalHypothesis (A=>?B, plausible provisional hypothesis), CausalKnowledge (A->B, accepted under an explicit causal model and evidence).

a_rows_sample.anchor: CausalNarrative\neq CausalKnowledge ... an LLM ... The deployment caused the outage ... must represent CausalHypothesis rather than silently converting it to CausalFact
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that an LLM's narrative causal claim ('the deployment caused the outage') must be represented as CausalHypothesis, not silently converted to CausalFact — CausalNarrative ≠ CausalKnowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: X_i=f_i(PA_i,U_i) ... Outage=f(Upgrade,FirewallChange,Load,UnknownFactors) ... genuine causal modeling rather than merely temporal reasoning
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a structural causal model X_i=f_i(PA_i,U_i) (variable as function of causal parents and exogenous factors), worked as Outage=f(Upgrade,FirewallChange,Load,UnknownFactors) with an accompanying causal graph.

a_rows_sample.anchor: G=(V,E) ... A\rightarrow B represents a causal hypothesis/model relation ... CausalGraph\neq ObservedWorld. It is a model of the world
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the causal graph G=(V,E) where an edge represents a causal hypothesis/model relation, not automatically empirical truth — CausalGraph ≠ ObservedWorld.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Corr(X,Y)\neq0 ... IceCreamSales\uparrow and DrowningDeaths\uparrow ... Temperature\rightarrow both ... the classic confounding problem
a_rows_sample.statement: The classic ice-cream/drowning/temperature confounding example: nonzero correlation does not establish causation since a common cause (temperature) may drive both variables.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C\rightarrow A and C\rightarrow B ... A and B may appear associated even if A\nrightarrow B ... ConfounderCandidate ... especially important for root-cause analysis
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes confounding (C->A and C->B can produce apparent A-B association absent direct causation), requiring KnowledgeOS to represent ConfounderCandidate, especially relevant for root-cause analysis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The earliest event before the failure is the root cause. That is wrong ... RootCause\neq EarliestPrecedingEvent
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects the naive 'earliest preceding event is the root cause' algorithm with a multi-step deployment/drift/firewall-change/outage timeline having several possible causal chains — RootCause ≠ EarliestPrecedingEvent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: do(X=x) ... P(Y\mid do(X=x)) ... differs from P(Y\mid X=x) ... foundational to modern causal inference
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces Pearl's intervention operator do(X=x) and the distinction P(Y|do(X=x)) vs P(Y|X=x) — 'foundational to modern causal inference.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(Outage\mid Upgrade)=0.2 ... does not necessarily mean P(Outage\mid do(Upgrade))=0.2 ... upgrades may occur precisely when systems already have problems
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example showing observational P(Outage|Upgrade) can diverge from interventional P(Outage|do(Upgrade)) because upgrades may be non-randomly timed relative to existing problems.

a_rows_sample.anchor: does not always need interventions ... Observational evidence, Controlled experiment, Natural experiment, Simulation ... each should be explicitly typed
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes causal reasoning does not always require real-world interventions, listing observational evidence, controlled experiment, natural experiment, and simulation as distinct, explicitly-typed evidence sources.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CausalEvidenceType\in\{Observational,Experimental,QuasiExperimental,Simulation,StructuralModel,ExpertAssessment\} ... should not have identical evidential status
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a six-value CausalEvidenceType taxonomy, explicitly not carrying identical evidential status across types.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ATE=E[Y\mid do(X=1)]-E[Y\mid do(X=0)] ... substantially stronger causal evidence than simple correlation ... even randomized experiments have assumptions and limitations
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the average treatment effect via random assignment, noting it is substantially stronger evidence than correlation but still carries assumptions/limitations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: \tau=Y(1)-Y(0) ... Usually we cannot observe both simultaneously. This is the fundamental causal inference problem
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines individual causal effect tau=Y(1)-Y(0) via potential outcomes, noting both cannot usually be jointly observed — 'the fundamental causal inference problem.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)] ... CausalEstimate: treatment/outcome/estimand/value/interval/model ... the model must be explicit
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)] as computable from appropriate designs, with a structured CausalEstimate record (treatment, outcome, estimand, value, interval, model) requiring an explicit model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Y_{do(X=0)} ... Y(0)=? ... generally not directly observable ... counterfactual conclusions require a model
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the counterfactual query (what would have happened under a different intervention, Y_do(X=0)), noting it is generally unobservable directly and requires a model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ObservedFact\neq Counterfactual ... Without the upgrade, the outage would not have happened must be typed as CounterfactualClaim ... should never silently enter the system as an observed fact
a_rows_sample.statement: States the critical distinction ObservedFact ≠ Counterfactual: a counterfactual statement must be typed CounterfactualClaim and never silently enter as an observed fact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: causal_confidence=0.93 unless the meaning is specified ... CausalAssessment=(Model,Assumptions,Data,Estimand,Estimate,Uncertainty)
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a bare causal_confidence score, requiring a structured CausalAssessment=(Model,Assumptions,Data,Estimand,Estimate,Uncertainty).

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(Y\mid do(X))=\sum_z P(Y\mid X,z)P(z) ... Identifiable=False ... this should become an explicit state
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces the identification concept: given sufficient adjustment variables Z, P(Y|do(X)) can sometimes be computed from observational data (backdoor-style formula) under appropriate causal assumptions; when no valid identification strategy exists, Identifiable=False must be an explicit state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: If Identifiable=False, Sarathi should not manufacture a causal answer ... Zero=NeedCausalEvidence ... Lord can then determine whether experiment/observation/simulation/expert review could reduce the gap
a_rows_sample.statement: States that non-identifiability feeds Zero=NeedCausalEvidence rather than a manufactured causal answer, letting Lord select experiment/additional observation/simulation/expert review as gap-reducing actions — 'fits our architecture beautifully.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Confidence_total = Confidence_1 x Confidence_2 x Confidence_3 ... That is generally wrong
b_rows_sample.statement: Rejects naive multiplication of stage confidences as generally wrong; the correct propagation depends on uncertainty semantics and dependence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Measurement uncertainty, Sampling uncertainty, Parameter uncertainty, Model uncertainty, Prediction uncertainty, Epistemic uncertainty, Aleatory variability ... must not automatically be collapsed into one number
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes at least seven kinds of uncertainty that must not be collapsed into one number.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Aleatory variability: Variation inherent in the phenomenon ... Epistemic uncertainty: Uncertainty caused by incomplete knowledge ... Randomness != LackOfKnowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the aleatory-vs-epistemic distinction with a travel-time/traffic example, giving the principle Randomness != LackOfKnowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Y=X+epsilon ... E[epsilon]=0 and Var(epsilon)=sigma^2 ... those assumptions themselves require justification
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes a basic measurement-error model and warns its moment assumptions require justification.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Y=h(X,theta,epsilon) ... KnowledgeOS should preserve the measurement model where available
b_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes to a measurement model KnowledgeOS should preserve, else downstream models may treat measured values as exact.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Var(Y) approx J Sigma J^T ... Jacobian ... covariance matrix ... exposes why independent multiplication of confidence values is inadequate
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes first-order error propagation via the Jacobian and covariance matrix.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Cov(X_i,X_j) != 0 ... Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y) ... Dependence matters
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes covariance's role in propagation, giving the principle that dependence matters.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_1 and E_2 both come from the same underlying report. Treating them as independent could artificially increase certainty. This is a major risk in AI systems
b_rows_sample.statement: States the evidence-duplication problem as a major risk in AI systems.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_1=f(S), E_2=g(S) ... E_1 not-perp E_2 ... combining them as independent evidence is invalid
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes correlated evidence sharing a common source and invalidates treating it as independent.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Provenance -> DependenceStructure -> CorrectUncertaintyPropagation ... This is a major result
b_rows_sample.statement: States provenance's mathematical role: it enables estimating dependency and hence correct uncertainty propagation, called a major result.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E) ... prior P(H) and likelihood P(E|H) must have explicit provenance and assumptions
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates Bayesian updating and requires explicit provenance/assumptions for prior and likelihood.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Not every knowledge problem has a meaningful prior ... BayesianUpdate must be a typed operation requiring a valid probabilistic model. It should not be the universal inference engine
b_rows_sample.statement: Constrains Bayesian updating to be a typed operation requiring a valid model, not a universal inference engine.

b_rows_sample.anchor: confidence intervals; sampling distributions; hypothesis tests; bootstrap distributions; asymptotic approximations ... theta-hat +- z SE(theta-hat) ... KnowledgeOS should preserve the framework
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists frequentist uncertainty representations and requires preserving the inferential framework used.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A standard confidence interval [L,U] should not automatically be interpreted as P(L<=theta<=U)=0.95. That interpretation is generally Bayesian, not classical frequentist
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns against the common misinterpretation of a frequentist confidence interval as a Bayesian probability statement.

b_rows_sample.anchor: X in [L,U] ... Latency in [100ms,150ms] ... No probability distribution is required
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines interval uncertainty requiring no probability distribution, with a latency example.

b_rows_sample.anchor: X in S where S is a feasible set ... useful when evidence constrains the possibilities without assigning probabilities
b_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes interval uncertainty to set-valued uncertainty over a feasible set.

b_rows_sample.anchor: X in [0,100] but have no justified distribution. The system should not invent X~Uniform(0,100) ... Bounded != Probabilistically Specified
b_rows_sample.statement: Forbids inventing a uniform distribution over a bounded but unjustified range, giving the principle Bounded != Probabilistically Specified.

b_rows_sample.anchor: theta in Theta_I ... PartiallyIdentified. This is stronger than simply saying uncertain
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces partial identification as a distinct, stronger-than-generic-uncertainty statistical concept.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 10<=X<=20 and Y=2X ... 20<=Y<=40 ... propagated a set-valued constraint without inventing a probability distribution
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example of set-valued constraint propagation without inventing a distribution.

b_rows_sample.anchor: X_1,X_2 -> Y -> Z ... KnowledgeOS should preserve DependencyGraph. Then uncertainty can be propagated through the graph
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a dependency graph structure for propagating uncertainty through a network.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
A temporal sequence, correlation, dependency, logical implication, and causation are not the same thing. Correlation
eq Dependency
eq Causation
eq Logical Implication
a_rows_sample.statement: States the governing principle: Correlation ≠ Dependency ≠ Causation ≠ Logical Implication must all be kept distinct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Suppose we observe A\rightarrow B ... Nexus became unavailable after a firewall change ... a simultaneous deployment; a certificate expiration; DNS failure; host failure; database failure. TemporalSequence\not\Rightarrow Causation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against inferring causation from mere temporal sequence (firewall change followed by Nexus unavailability), listing five alternative explanations — TemporalSequence ⇏ Causation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Four different relations ... Logical implication P\rightarrow Q ... x=2\Rightarrow x^2=4 ... Dependency P\rightsquigarrow Q ... BackupConfiguration\rightsquigarrow BackupExecution ... Correlation P\sim Q ... Causation P\rightsquigarrow_c Q ... Changing P, under a specified causal model and intervent
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines four distinct relations: Logical implication (P→Q, formal entailment), Dependency (P⇝Q, process-model dependence), Correlation (P~Q, statistical association), and Causation (P⇝_c Q, intervention changes the effect's distribution) as the strongest and substantially different relation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Causality requires a model ... We cannot determine causality merely from Data. We need CausalModel. Cause_M(X,Y) is meaningful relative to M. Causality is model relative.
a_rows_sample.statement: States causality cannot be determined from data alone; Cause_M(X,Y) is only meaningful relative to an explicit causal model M — causality is model-relative.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Structural causal model ... M=(V,U,F,P(U)) ... observed/endogenous variables; exogenous variables; structural equations; distribution over exogenous variables. Availability = f(Firewall,DNS,Certificate,Host,Database,U). This expresses a causal hypothesis.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a structural causal model M=(V,U,F,P(U)) worked with an Availability=f(Firewall,DNS,Certificate,Host,Database,U) hypothesis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Causal graph ... FirewallChange\rightarrow Connectivity\rightarrow NexusAvailability ... CertificateExpiry\rightarrow NexusAvailability ... HostFailure\rightarrow NexusAvailability. This is a causal hypothesis/model, not automatically established fact.
a_rows_sample.statement: Constructs a worked causal graph with three converging paths to NexusAvailability, explicitly labeled a hypothesis/model, not established fact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Causal edges need epistemic status ... X\rightarrow_cY must itself be knowledge. CausalRelation=(Cause,Effect,Model,Evidence,Support,Uncertainty,Context,Validity). A causal relation is itself an epistemically governed object.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines CausalRelation=(Cause,Effect,Model,Evidence,Support,Uncertainty,Context,Validity) — a causal edge must itself be an epistemically governed object, not a bare fact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence for causality ... controlled experiments; interventions; natural experiments; temporal evidence; mechanism evidence; statistical data; domain rules; simulations; observational studies. CausalEvidence\neq ordinary co-occurrence.
a_rows_sample.statement: Lists nine kinds of causal evidence of varying strength, distinguishing CausalEvidence from ordinary co-occurrence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Intervention ... do(X=x). Then P(Y\mid do(X=x)) can differ from P(Y\mid X=x). This is the mathematical distinction between intervention and observation. ... Observation\neq Intervention. We observed that systems with firewall rule X are unavailable is P(Y\mid X). We changed the firewall rule to X an
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces do(X=x) intervention notation, distinguishing P(Y|do(X=x)) from mere observational P(Y|X=x) — Observation ≠ Intervention, worked with a firewall-rule example.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Counterfactual reasoning ... Y_{X=x} represents a potential/counterfactual outcome under intervention X=x. Y_{X=1} versus Y_{X=0}. If Y_{X=1}\neq Y_{X=0}, the causal model attributes an effect to X. ... Counterfactuals are not observations ... Counterfactual(P)\neq Observed(P). A counterfactual is g
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines counterfactual potential outcomes Y_{X=x} (worked with Y_{X=1} vs Y_{X=0}) and states Counterfactual(P) ≠ Observed(P), tagged Acquisition=CounterfactualInference with provenance including causal model, assumptions, evidence, intervention, and inference method.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Why this matters for KnowledgeOS ... What happens if we migrate Nexus without parallel operation? KnowledgeOS cannot simply search documents for an answer. CurrentKnowledge \rightarrow CausalModel \rightarrow Intervention \rightarrow Simulation/Inference \rightarrow CounterfactualOutcome. That is a
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues answering a what-if migration question requires the full CausalModel→Intervention→Simulation/Inference→CounterfactualOutcome pipeline — fundamentally different from document retrieval.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Causal model versus domain dependency ... BackupConfiguration\rightsquigarrow BackupExecution ... does not automatically prove BackupConfiguration\rightarrow_c SuccessfulRestore. storage failure; permission failure; corrupted backup; restore procedure failure. ProcessDependency\neq CausalSufficiency
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows process dependency (configuration→execution) does not establish causal sufficiency for the ultimate outcome (successful restore) given other failure modes — ProcessDependency ≠ CausalSufficiency.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
Necessary and sufficient causes ... Necessary cause 
eg X\Rightarrow
eg Y ... Sufficient cause X\Rightarrow Y ... Contributory cause P(Y\mid do(X))>P(Y\mid do(
eg X)). KnowledgeOS should not reduce them to one generic causes relation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines three distinct causal-strength notions — Necessary (¬X⇒¬Y), Sufficient (X⇒Y), Contributory (P(Y|do(X))>P(Y|do(¬X))) — that must not be collapsed into one generic causes relation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Multiple causes ... X_1,X_2,X_3\rightarrow Y ... DNSFailure \lor CertificateFailure \lor NetworkFailure \rightarrow ServiceUnavailable. But the logical form is not necessarily X_1\lor X_2\lor X_3. The actual causal mechanism might be Y=f(X_1,X_2,X_3,U). Therefore the causal model must explicitly def
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows a multi-cause outage example where the true mechanism f(X1,X2,X3,U) need not reduce to a simple disjunction, requiring the causal model to explicitly define the mechanism.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Causal uncertainty ... Causal relation: Candidate ... Support: Moderate ... Alternative causes: DNS failure, Certificate expiry ... Uncertainty: High. Not: Firewall change caused the outage. Hypothesis\neq AcceptedFact.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires a structured Candidate-status causal record (support, alternative causes, uncertainty) rather than an assertive causal claim — reaffirming Hypothesis ≠ AcceptedFact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Competing causal models ... M_1: Firewall\rightarrow Failure and M_2: Certificate\rightarrow Failure. KnowledgeOS may retain both M_1,M_2. They are competing hypotheses. This is analogous to the contradictory assertion model from Step 9. CausalModel competition can be represented without premature s
a_rows_sample.statement: Allows retaining multiple competing causal models simultaneously without premature selection, analogous to Step 9's paraconsistent handling of contradictory assertions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Lord can use causal models ... M1 predicts: firewall logs contain denied traffic ... M2 predicts: certificate errors appear in service logs ... M3 predicts: host health checks fail. Then Lord selects the next evidence acquisition based on expected information gain. This connects Step 14 directly to
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes causal diagnosis as active learning: q*=argmax_q ExpectedInformationGain(q) subject to Cost(q)≤Budget, with Lord selecting evidence that best distinguishes competing causal models (M1/M2/M3 each predicting different observable evidence) — connecting to Step 6's VOE machinery.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi's role ... Inspect firewall logs. Check certificate. Test DNS. Check host health. Sārathi considers risk; cost; urgency; authority; operational safety. Sārathi\rightarrow NextInvestigation. Zero: What is wrong/unknown? Lord: What could explain/reduce it? Sārathi: What should we do next?
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends Zero/Lord/Sārathi to causal diagnosis, with Sārathi weighing risk/cost/urgency/authority/safety to select NextInvestigation among Lord's candidate diagnostic actions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Causal reasoning and discrepancy ... CauseOfIncident must be known with Support\geq Strong. Current state: Cause=Candidate. Then \Delta_{causal} exists. Lord can search for interventions or observations that reduce it.
a_rows_sample.statement: Connects unresolved causal attribution to a first-class discrepancy Δ_causal that Lord can act on to reduce.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Causal model validation ... A model can explain historical observations while being causally wrong. Therefore we need ModelValidation. out-of-sample predictions; interventions; controlled tests; natural experiments; mechanism verification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against accepting a causal model merely because it explains existing data (overfitting risk), requiring ModelValidation via out-of-sample prediction, intervention, controlled tests, natural experiments, or mechanism verification.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
When can KnowledgeOS legitimately say: We know enough to proceed? That is fundamentally different from saying We know everything. ... complete knowledge is generally impossible. ... The correct concept is purpose-relative sufficiency. ... Truth
eq Knowledge
eq Completeness
eq Sufficiency ... Suff
b_rows_sample.statement: States the governing principle of purpose-relative sufficiency (not universal completeness), separating five concepts: Truth ≠ Knowledge ≠ Completeness ≠ Sufficiency ≠ DecisionReadiness.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Truth ... Truth(P) ... KnowledgeOS generally cannot directly determine this for arbitrary propositions. It can determine Supported(P) or Accepted(P). Accepted(P)\not\Rightarrow Truth(P). This remains one of our foundational invariants.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Accepted(P) ⇏ Truth(P) as a foundational invariant, since KnowledgeOS cannot generally determine Truth(P) directly for arbitrary propositions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Completeness ... K_t=I^K_{P_r} ... this is usually unrealistic. There may always be unknown information; future changes; unmodeled dimensions; irrelevant details. Absolute completeness is generally not required.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues absolute completeness (K_t=I^K_{P_r}) is generally unrealistic and not required, given always-possible unknown information, future change, unmodeled dimensions, and irrelevant details.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Purpose-relative completeness ... \mathcal Q(P_r) containing everything that must be known for purpose P_r. Purpose: migrate Nexus. Q_1=CurrentVersion, Q_2=HostIdentity, Q_3=NetworkDependencies, Q_4=FirewallRules, Q_5=BackupCapability, Q_6=CertificateStatus ... Completeness(K_t,P_r) = coverage of Q(
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a purpose-relative requirement set Q(P_r) (illustrated with six Nexus-migration requirements) and Completeness(K_t,P_r) as coverage of that set.

b_rows_sample.anchor: But coverage is not enough ... all six questions have answers ... BackupStatus=Contested. The knowledge coverage is high, but the state may not be safe enough for migration. Coverage\neq Sufficiency.
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows full requirement coverage can still be insufficient (e.g. a contested backup status), establishing Coverage ≠ Sufficiency.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Epistemic sufficiency ... Sufficient_\rho(K_t,P_r) ... The current Knowledge State satisfies the minimum epistemic requirements necessary for purpose P_r, according to policy \rho. Sufficient_\rho = f(Coverage,Support,Uncertainty,Conflict,Validity,Criticality). The function is policy-defined.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Sufficient_ρ(K_t,P_r) as a policy-defined function of Coverage, Support, Uncertainty, Conflict, Validity, and Criticality — not coverage alone.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Requirement-level evaluation ... q=(Target,Condition,MinimumEpistemicState,Context,Criticality) ... Target = BackupCapability, Condition = RestoreTestSuccessful, MinimumSupport = Strong, Conflict = None, Validity = Current, Criticality = High.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a KnowledgeRequirement q=(Target,Condition,MinimumEpistemicState,Context,Criticality), worked with a BackupCapability/RestoreTestSuccessful example.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Requirement satisfaction ... Satisfies(K_t,q)\in\{True,False,Unknown\} ... Backup restore test: Unknown does not mean False. Unknown\neq False. This continues our open-world principle.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines three-valued Satisfies(K_t,q)∈{True,False,Unknown}, reaffirming Unknown≠False as continuing the open-world principle.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Three-valued requirement evaluation ... \mathbb T_3=\{Satisfied,Unsatisfied,Unknown\} ... Current version known Satisfied ... Backup restore tested Unknown ... Firewall dependencies known Unsatisfied. Now the overall readiness can be evaluated.
b_rows_sample.statement: Works a worked requirement table (version/owner Satisfied, backup-restore Unknown, firewall-dependencies Unsatisfied) illustrating T_3={Satisfied,Unsatisfied,Unknown}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Critical requirements ... Criticality(q)\in\{Low,Medium,High,Critical\} ... Critical(q)=True \land Satisfies(K,q)\neq Satisfied means NotReady. Thus a single unresolved critical requirement may block an action even when 95% of the knowledge is complete.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Criticality(q) and the rule that any unsatisfied Critical requirement forces NotReady regardless of overall coverage percentage.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This is why scalar completeness is dangerous ... Coverage=95% ... perhaps the missing 5% is: Does the backup actually restore? Then 95% may still mean NotReady. Percentage completeness cannot replace requirement-level evaluation. A scalar can be useful as a summary, but never as the fundamental deci
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns a high percentage-completeness score (95%) can still mean NotReady if the missing fraction is the critical requirement — scalar completeness must never replace requirement-level evaluation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sufficiency vector ... \mathbf S(K_t,P_r) = (s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n) where each s_i=Satisfies(K_t,q_i). This preserves the individual deficiencies. \mathbf S=(1,1,1,0,?,1)
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a sufficiency vector S(K_t,P_r)=(s1,...,sn) over per-requirement satisfaction values, preserving individual deficiencies rather than collapsing to a scalar.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision readiness ... Ready_\rho(K_t,P_r) ... This is not purely epistemic. It can depend on epistemic sufficiency; risk; authority; constraints; policy; operational conditions. DecisionReadiness = f(EpistemicSufficiency,Risk,Authority,Constraints,Purpose,Policy).
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines DecisionReadiness=f(EpistemicSufficiency,Risk,Authority,Constraints,Purpose,Policy) as broader than epistemic sufficiency alone.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Example ... 92% coverage ... Critical uncertainty: Backup restore test unknown ... Risk: High ... Authority: Architecture Board ... Policy: Migration requires verified recovery ... Sufficient=False and Ready=False. Lord should propose: Perform restore test. Sārathi should recommend: Do not proceed u
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked migration-readiness example (92% coverage, critical uncertainty, high risk) producing Sufficient=False and Ready=False, with Lord/Sārathi recommending the restore test before proceeding.

b_rows_sample.anchor: But sometimes action is allowed despite uncertainty ... Criticality=Medium ... the business accepts the risk. Then Sufficient=False but Ready=True may still be possible if AcceptRisk=True. Epistemic insufficiency does not always imply operational prohibition. Instead the organization may explicitly
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows Sufficient=False can still coexist with Ready=True given explicit risk acceptance at Medium criticality — epistemic insufficiency does not always imply operational prohibition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This creates a crucial separation ... Epistemic decision Do we know enough? Sufficient? ... Governance decision Are we authorized to proceed despite the remaining gap? Authorized? ... Operational decision Should we execute? Ready? ... Sufficient\neq Authorized\neq Ready. This is an extremely importa
b_rows_sample.statement: Draws a three-way DDD boundary between Epistemic (Sufficient?), Governance (Authorized?), and Operational (Ready?) decisions — Sufficient ≠ Authorized ≠ Ready.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Risk acceptance ... q_4=Unknown. But an authorized body explicitly accepts the risk: RiskAccepted(q_4). Then Ready may become true. But KnowledgeOS must retain q_4=Unknown. It must never transform RiskAccepted into Known. RiskAcceptance does not eliminate epistemic uncertainty.
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires RiskAcceptance never eliminate the underlying epistemic uncertainty: an accepted-risk requirement remains recorded Unknown even when Ready becomes True — RiskAcceptance does not eliminate epistemic uncertainty.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This gives us a powerful distinction ... The Architecture Board says: Proceed anyway; risk accepted. KnowledgeOS should record KnowledgeGap=True and RiskAccepted=True. Not KnowledgeGap=False. This is exactly the kind of distinction an enterprise knowledge system needs.
b_rows_sample.statement: Illustrates recording both KnowledgeGap=True and RiskAccepted=True simultaneously (never collapsing the gap to False) after an authorized risk-accepted proceed decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Ideal State revisited ... Relevant_\rho(d,P_r) ... \Delta_t^{P_r} = \{d\in\Delta_t\mid Relevant_\rho(d,P_r)\}. This gives us a purpose-specific discrepancy. ... Purpose-specific Ideal State ... I_t(P_r) ... I_t(Migration) differs from I_t(Audit). ... Completeness becomes purpose-relative ... Complet
b_rows_sample.statement: Redefines the Ideal State and discrepancy as purpose-relative — I_t(P_r) and Δ_t^{P_r}=Relevant_ρ(d,P_r)-filtered — concluding there is no universal 'complete knowledge', only knowledge sufficient for a specified purpose under specified conditions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Readiness as a predicate ... Ready_\rho(K_t,P_r) \iff \forall q\in Q(P_r): RequirementCondition_\rho(K_t,q) with exceptions for explicitly authorized risk acceptance. ... Ready_\rho = Policy_\rho(RequirementStates,RiskAcceptances,Authority,Constraints). ... No universal readiness formula ... Ready=0
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Ready_ρ as a universally-quantified requirement predicate with risk-acceptance exceptions, generalized to Ready_ρ=Policy_ρ(RequirementStates,RiskAcceptances,Authority,Constraints), explicitly warning against a scalar formula like Ready=0.95×KnowledgeScore as a serious theoretical mistake.

a_aliases: Step 14: Causality, Dependency, and Counterfactual Reasoning
b_aliases: Step 13: Sufficiency, Completeness, and Readiness for Purpose

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'causal-dependency-counterfactual-reasoning' POSSIBLY relates to 'sufficiency-completeness-decision-readiness' (batch B0021). Note: S0870's Step 14: Pearl-style causal machinery (structural causal model, do-calculus, counterfactuals) integrated as a CausalReasoning bounded context; separates Correlation/Dependency/Causation/LogicalImplication; PredictiveModel!=CausalModel; competing causal models retained without premature selection; causal diagnosis as active learning connecting to Step 6's VOE; twelve CA1-CA12 invariants; hands off to Step 15 (decision theory / action selection / Sarathi).

a_rows_sample.anchor: causal inference compares outcomes in the same population under different interventions, whereas association compares different subsets of the population based on what actually happened.
a_rows_sample.statement: Observational Knowledge (X correlated with Y) and Causal Knowledge (intervention on X changes Y) must never have the same epistemic status; 'Teams using architecture reviews had fewer production incidents' is not equivalent to 'Introducing architecture reviews reduces production incidents', the latter requiring causal assumptions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: an effect requires specifying the outcome, the actions being compared and the population. ... CausalQuestion: population, intervention, comparator, outcome, time horizon, estimand
a_rows_sample.statement: CausalQuestion object formalized with population/intervention/comparator/outcome/time_horizon/estimand fields, replacing an unconstrained 'Does X affect Y?' question, illustrated with an example (projects using KnowledgeOS; mandatory architecture review vs none; architecture-related production defects; 12 months; average causal risk difference); called 'an epistemic schema', not merely a statistical method.

a_rows_sample.anchor: individual causal effect through the difference between Y1 = outcome if intervention happens and Y0 = outcome if intervention does not happen ... normally only one of these outcomes is observed for each individual.
a_rows_sample.statement: Counterfactual Lens: KnowledgeOS should represent causal claims as counterfactual claims (observed evidence + counterfactual estimand + identifying assumptions), not ordinary observations, since the counterfactual outcome (what defect rate a project would have had without an intervention) is never directly observed; proposed for first-class representation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: causal diagrams to identify common causes/confounding, conditioning on common effects/selection bias, measurement bias, effect modification ... KnowledgeOS should distinguish semantic relationships from causal relationships.
a_rows_sample.statement: Causal Graph Lens: a causal graph (directed edges with confounding/selection/measurement structure) differs fundamentally from an ordinary semantic knowledge-graph 'related_to' edge; proposes a distinct CausalGraph construct with explicit edge semantics rather than adding a bare 'causes' edge to the existing graph.

a_rows_sample.anchor: confounding as arising when treatment and outcome share common causes. ... CAUSAL CLAIM REVIEW ... Exchangeability: NOT ESTABLISHED ... Causal conclusion: ABSTAIN
a_rows_sample.statement: Confounding Lens as a first-class anti-false-inference mechanism, illustrated by 'experienced teams' confounding an architecture-review-vs-quality relationship; a CAUSAL CLAIM REVIEW output lists observed association, potential confounders (team maturity, project size, engineering leadership), exchangeability status, and a resulting ABSTAIN conclusion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: conditioning on common effects can produce selection bias, and even randomization does not protect against selection bias occurring after randomization. ... Why are these observations present in the evidence set?
a_rows_sample.statement: Selection-Bias Lens: selecting evidence (e.g. only successful projects) before inference can bias conclusions ('Architecture practice X works') even without explicit randomization failure; KnowledgeOS should ask why observations are present in the evidence set at all.

a_rows_sample.anchor: measurement error can make the observed association differ from the causal effect ... The observation mechanism itself becomes part of the evidence model.
a_rows_sample.statement: Measurement-Bias Lens maps to observation provenance: Reality -> Observation mechanism -> Stored evidence -> Statistical inference, with the observation mechanism itself becoming part of the evidence model, since exchangeability/positivity/consistency alone are insufficient when variables are measured incorrectly.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the relevant combinations of treatment and covariates actually occur in the population. ... Claim scope = ALL teams / Evidence support = narrow population -> POSITIVITY / GENERALISABILITY WARNING
a_rows_sample.statement: Positivity/Coverage Lens becomes an Evidence Coverage Check: a claim's scope (e.g. 'all teams') must be checked against actual evidence coverage (e.g. only large Java teams), producing a positivity/generalisability warning when scope exceeds coverage.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the observed outcome under the treatment actually received corresponds to the relevant counterfactual outcome. ... If 'treatment X' has multiple uncontrolled versions, the causal question itself may be ill-defined.
a_rows_sample.statement: Consistency Lens: the intervention must be sufficiently well-defined that 'X happened' has a single meaning (contrast vague 'AI governance' with a precisely versioned 'AI governance policy v1.3 + mandatory architecture review + defined approval workflow + defined enforcement mechanism'), connecting causal consistency to ubiquitous-language/bounded-semantics concerns.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Intervention: DO(X) ... OBSERVE -> HYPOTHESIZE -> INTERVENE -> OBSERVE OUTCOME -> UPDATE CAUSAL EVIDENCE ... KnowledgeOS becomes capable of supporting organizational learning, not merely document retrieval.
a_rows_sample.statement: Intervention Lens: represent claims as do(X) interventions with expected outcome and counterfactual, enabling an OBSERVE->HYPOTHESIZE->INTERVENE->OBSERVE OUTCOME->UPDATE CAUSAL EVIDENCE loop that supports organizational learning rather than mere document retrieval.

a_rows_sample.anchor: time-varying treatments, time-varying confounders, treatment-confounder feedback ... treatment-confounder feedback can make traditional adjustment methods biased even when the relevant confounders are measured.
a_rows_sample.statement: Time-Varying Knowledge Lens: KnowledgeOS is inherently longitudinal (X0->Y0->X1->Y1->X2->Y2, earlier decisions affecting later evidence), so a naive single-step X->Y model is often insufficient, echoing the book's warning that treatment-confounder feedback can bias traditional adjustment even with measured confounders.

a_rows_sample.anchor: variable selection for causal inference is difficult and recommend multiple sensitivity analyses rather than pretending there is one universally correct selection procedure. ... ROBUST CAUSAL CONCLUSION or CAUSAL CONCLUSION SENSITIVE TO ASSUMPTIONS
a_rows_sample.statement: Sensitivity/Triangulation Lens (called 'one of the strongest principles in the entire book'): run multiple methods/alternative assumptions/alternative causal graphs over the same evidence and check convergence, yielding either a ROBUST CAUSAL CONCLUSION or a CAUSAL CONCLUSION SENSITIVE TO ASSUMPTIONS, rather than a single model producing a single answer.

a_rows_sample.anchor: predictive ML variable selection is not equivalent to causal variable selection ... ML can be combined with causal inference through doubly robust estimators, but ML does not magically solve confounding or uncertainty.
a_rows_sample.statement: Machine Learning Lens correction: 'Prediction != causal inference' proposed as a KnowledgeOS architectural invariant, because predicting treatment well is not the same as including variables necessary for exchangeability, and unnecessary variables can increase variance or create positivity problems.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS SHALL NOT promote an associational finding to a causal claim without an explicit causal question, identified intervention and comparator, declared causal assumptions, an identifiability assessment, and an appropriate uncertainty/sensitivity assessment. ... KnowledgeOS SHALL preserve the distinction between predictive validity and causal validity.
a_rows_sample.statement: Two proposed KnowledgeOS constitutional principles synthesizing both books: (1) no promotion of an associational finding to a causal claim without explicit causal question/intervention/comparator/assumptions/identifiability assessment/uncertainty-sensitivity assessment; (2) preserve the distinction between predictive validity and causal validity, since predictive and causal models serve different purposes and predictive variable selection can be inappropriate for causal inference.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Before choosing a statistical method, determine what question you are actually trying to answer and whether that question is identifiable from the available evidence under explicit assumptions. ... KnowledgeOS needs a formal taxonomy of claim types and corresponding inference obligations.
a_rows_sample.statement: Synthesizes both source books into a single QUESTION -> {Descriptive|Associational|Causal} -> (for Causal) Identification -> {Estimation|Abstain} -> Uncertainty -> Robustness -> Sensitivity Analysis -> Epistemic Status decision hierarchy; concludes KnowledgeOS should become an 'Evidence Reasoning System with explicit statistical and causal epistemics' rather than a generic AI/ML analytics engine, and flags a formal taxonomy of claim types with corresponding inference obligations as the next architectural research step.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Do not automatically turn every noun into a domain object. ... conceptual richness does not prove a software bounded context.
a_rows_sample.statement: DDD warning applied to the causal vocabulary extracted from the book (Causal Question, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome, Population, Time Zero, Counterfactual, Causal Effect, Assumption, Exchangeability, Positivity, Consistency, Confounder, Mediator, Collider, Selection, Measurement, Estimand, Identification, Estimation, Sensitivity, Evidence): ownership, lifecycle, invariants, decisions, consistency boundaries, language and dependencies must be discovered before any noun becomes a domain object.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Book of Evidence tells us HOW observations become evidence ... Causal Inference tells us HOW evidence supports causal claims ... Statistical methods tell us HOW evidence is quantified ... DDD tells us HOW to model the domain ... Wisdom tells us HOW to determine what evidence is needed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Combines all four books+lenses into one epistemic operating loop: Decision -> Evidence Need -> Evidence Question -> Acquisition Design -> {Selection Procedure, Measurement Procedure, Context Conditions} -> Observation -> Acquisition Audit -> Candidate Evidence -> Evidence Assessment -> Statistical Analysis -> Causal Assessment -> Knowledge -> Wisdom -> Decision, described as 'starting to look like the actual KnowledgeOS epistemic operating loop.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: We should not conclude: 'Everything in KnowledgeOS should be Bayesian.' ... Also: Bayesian ≠ causal. ... They interact ... But they are not the same thing.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit scope limits: Bayesian updating complements but does not replace deduction/causal inference/statistical estimation/formal verification/empirical testing/domain rules/logical constraints/governance/human judgment; and Bayesian belief-updating ('how should belief change given evidence?') is distinct from causal inference ('what would happen under intervention?') even though they interact in a chain Evidence->Bayesian update->belief in causal model->causal inference->decision.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Correlation between action and outcome does not establish causation (transition to Step 43)
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies a missing dimension beyond State/Evidence/Decision/Action/Outcome: correlation between action and outcome does not establish causation. If KnowledgeOS observes Action=A followed by Outcome=B, it cannot automatically conclude A->B -- especially important if KnowledgeOS is expected to learn from its own decisions. Opens Step 43 (Causal Reasoning, Intervention, Counterfactuals and Learning from Outcomes) with the central principle that an outcome following an action does not prove the action caused the outcome, framed as essential for KnowledgeOS to 'learn from engineering decisions rather than merely record them'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(Y|A) is not generally equal to P(Y|do(A))
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces the causal layer by formalizing the central distinction between Correlation and Causation as P(Y|A) not generally equal to P(Y|do(A)) -- called one of the most important mathematical foundations for an intelligent KnowledgeOS. Motivated by the premise that observing Action=A followed by Outcome=Y does not license concluding A->Y ('temporal sequence and correlation are not sufficient to establish causation').

b_rows_sample.anchor: Structural causal model X_i=f_i(Pa_i,U_i); CausalEdge != GenericRelationship; need for G_C
b_rows_sample.statement: Represents a structural causal model conceptually as X_i = f_i(Pa_i, U_i) (Pa_i = causal parents, U_i = exogenous factors), a mechanism-oriented representation rather than a purely correlational graph. Argues KnowledgeOS needs a distinct causal graph G_C alongside the existing knowledge-relationship graph G_K -- relatedTo does not mean causes, dependsOn does not necessarily mean causes -- formalized as CausalEdge != GenericRelationship.

b_rows_sample.anchor: CausalClaim tuple; causal generalization scope; causal edges are knowledge assertions not metaphysical truth
b_rows_sample.statement: A causal claim should carry a GeneralizationScope (e.g. {BusinessUnit, Technology, Environment, Time}) so an agent can judge whether it applies to the current situation. Gives the full CausalClaim tuple: (Cause, Effect, Mechanism, Evidence, StudyDesign, Assumptions, Scope, Time, EffectSize, Uncertainty, Model) -- 'a powerful domain object'. Distinguishes the causal graph G_C from the provenance/dependency graph G_P: a causal edge A->B should itself have provenance (Evidence -> CausalClaim(A->B)); the causal graph is not metaphysical truth -- an edge A->B is a knowledge assertion supported by evidence, so CausalEdge is in K.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 43 verdict, six core principles, and G_C as a new graph type alongside G_K/G_I/G_P
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 43 -- PASS and restates six core principles: Correlation != Causation; Observation != Intervention; Temporal precedence != Causality; Prediction != Explanation; Counterfactual != Observation; Causal claims require assumptions. Adds a new mathematical layer G_C (causal graph) to the architecture's existing graph family: G_K (knowledge relationships), G_I (identity relationships), G_P (provenance/dependency), and now G_C (causal relationships) -- 'these graphs interact but have different semantics'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Provenance and Causality reduced to typed relations; Supports != Causes != DependsOn
b_rows_sample.statement: Provenance Prov(C)={E_1,...,E_n}, generalized to a DAG-shaped Prov(x); reduced to a relation, not a primitive object: Supports(E,C), DerivedFrom(C1,C2). Causality is another relation Causes(A,B), explicitly not to be conflated with Supports(A,B): Supports != Causes. Software dependency DependsOn(A,B) is yet another relation, and DependsOn != Causes -- a system may technically depend on a component without that component being the causal reason for a given outcome. Consolidates a typed relation set R={Supports, DependsOn, Causes, Identifies, MapsTo, Contradicts, Precedes} that must remain typed: collapsing everything into a generic RelatedTo(A,B) loses semantics and could let an AI infer RelatedTo=>Causes, 'recreating one of the fundamental problems we eliminated in Step 43'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge version graph G_K=(V,E); RevisionGraph != CausalGraph; candidate partial order tested for reflexivity/antisymmetry/transitivity
b_rows_sample.statement: Represents legitimate branching K1->K2^A and K1->K2^B (competing hypotheses) as a version graph G_K=(V,E) with V=KnowledgeStates and E=RevisionRelations, more general than a simple version chain; argues a revision graph should normally be acyclic (a revision should not causally depend on itself) while a domain may separately represent cyclic feedback elsewhere, distinguishing RevisionGraph from CausalGraph. Defines the candidate partial order K_A⪯K_B (K_B is a valid successor/refinement of K_A) and tests it for reflexivity (K_A⪯K_A), antisymmetry (K_A⪯K_B ∧ K_B⪯K_A ⇒ K_A=K_B under the chosen equivalence), and transitivity (K_A⪯K_B ∧ K_B⪯K_C ⇒ K_A⪯K_C).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Structural causal model re-derived (do(X=x) replaces the mechanism); generic-edge-collapse experiment FAILs, reinforcing typed relations
b_rows_sample.statement: Re-derives structural equations X=f_X(U_X), Y=f_Y(X,U_Y) with do(X=x) replacing X's mechanism (experiment 9: observing X=x does not block Z->Y, but do(X=x) removes the incoming mechanism into X -- DifferentCausalSemantics -- PASS), and the G_K (knowledge/dependency) vs G_C (causal) graph distinction. Experiment 10: using one generic 'A->B' edge type for dependency, provenance, temporal order, and causality simultaneously yields SemanticFailure -- explicitly FAIL, reinforcing the requirement for explicit relation types (DerivedFrom, DependsOn, Precedes, Supports, Contradicts, Causes, Authorizes) that must never be reduced to one generic arrow.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Trust non-transitivity; multi-graph model (G_K,G_P,G_D,G_A,G_T) not collapsible (generic-relation-schema FAILs)
b_rows_sample.statement: States trust transitivity is not universally valid: Trust(A,B)=High and Trust(B,C)=High does not license Trust(A,C)=High -- experiment 20 rejects that inference -- PASS, 'prevents dangerous trust propagation through agent networks'. Extends the multi-graph family with a Trust graph G_T alongside Knowledge (G_K), Provenance (G_P), Dependency (G_D), and Authority (G_A) graphs, which 'should not be collapsed into one universal graph'. Experiment 21: representing all relationships as one generic relation(source,target,type) with no bounded semantics yields SemanticAmbiguity -- explicitly FAIL, 'the relationships have different invariants' -- while noting a higher-level system may still correlate G_K/G_P/G_A while each retains its own domain semantics.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 94.35 — Provenance-aware knowledge graph ... Fact<-supportedBy-Evidence. Evidence-origin->Source. Source-trust->TrustAssessment.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a provenance-aware knowledge graph pattern: Fact←supportedBy—Evidence, Evidence—origin→Source, Source—trust→TrustAssessment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 101.21 — Architecture must be inferred from dependencies ... examine DependencyGraph. For each component C_i→C_j. Then compare the actual graph against the allowed architecture graph.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes inferring actual architecture from the code dependency graph, compared against the allowed architecture graph.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 101.36 — Architecture evidence graph ... G=(V,E) where nodes include Requirement, Principle, ADR, Component, CodeArtifact, Test, Deployment, RuntimeObservation. Edges: implements, verifies, dependsOn, deployedAs, observedBy.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the architecture evidence graph G=(V,E) with typed nodes (Requirement/Principle/ADR/Component/CodeArtifact/Test/Deployment/RuntimeObservation) and typed edges (implements/verifies/dependsOn/deployedAs/observedBy).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 102.60 — Architecture inventory as a graph ... G_architecture=(V,E) with nodes Repository, Component, BoundedContext, Schema, Policy, ADR, Test, Deployment, Runtime. Edges: contains, implements, dependsOn, governedBy, verifiedBy, deployedAs, observedBy.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the architecture inventory as a typed graph G_architecture=(V,E) with node types (Repository/Component/BoundedContext/Schema/Policy/ADR/Test/Deployment/Runtime) and edge types (contains/implements/dependsOn/governedBy/verifiedBy/deployedAs/observedBy).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 102.61 — Experiment 27 ... A critical component has no governedBy edge. Expected: governance gap. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 27: a critical component with no governedBy edge is a governance gap; result PASS.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 3 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: This document does NOT design the Kernel. It produces QUESTIONS, OBSERVATIONS, DISTINCTIONS, and FALSIFICATION TARGETS -- not architecture.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit methodological self-limitation: integrating Chinese philosophical traditions (Daoism/Confucianism/Mohism/Xunzi/Zhuangzi), Tarka-Nyaya (Annambhatta's Tarka-sangraha), and Audi's Western epistemology to interrogate assumptions underlying a minimal Knowledge Kernel produces questions/observations/distinctions/falsification targets only, explicitly not architecture or a kernel design.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Names are normative, not descriptive.
a_rows_sample.statement: Ten Chinese-tradition observations against the Kernel's Western assumptions: (1) names are normative not descriptive (Kongzi's zhengming), (2) identity is relational not intrinsic (Xunzi/Confucianism role-based identity), (3) change is continuous not discrete (Daoist hua vs discrete state transitions), (4) contradiction is not necessarily error (Zhuangzi perspectivalism: some contradictions are legitimate differing perspectives), (5) justification is practical (Mohist non-correspondence truth: a claim is true if it works), (6) context is constitutive not external (Zhuangzi/Xunzi), (7) knowing and acting are inseparable (Xunzi: knowledge as capacity not possession), (8) authority is relational/role-based (Confucianism), (9) continuity can be transformation (Zhuangzi: sameness via continuous process, not essence), (10) absence and withdrawal are different (Daoism) -- each posed as a challenge the Kernel's naming/identity/change/contradiction/justification/context/knowledge/authority/continuity/retraction treatment must answer.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Definition defects must be tested.
a_rows_sample.statement: Ten Tarka-Nyaya observations for testing the Kernel boundary: (11) a defining characteristic must avoid avyapti (under-covers), ativyapti (over-covers), asambhava (cannot apply); (12) reason must establish the conclusion via the paksa-sadhya-hetu discipline (proposition/reason/example/application/conclusion); (13) vyapti (invariable concomitance) must be tested in both directions (anvaya/vyatireka); (14) five defective reasons (savyabhicara/viruddha/satpratipaksa/asiddha/badhita) give precise argument-defect vocabulary; (15) absence claims need a counter-correlate (pratiyogi) and a specified kind of absence; (16) viparyaya (erroneous apprehension) shows representation is not truth -- the Kernel must not silently convert representation into semantic truth; (17) samsaya (doubt: mutually contradictory attributes in the same substratum) must be kept distinct from contradiction and error; (18) nigrahasthana (argument failure points) catalogs precise failure modes (abandoning/changing the proposition or reason, etc.); (19) the conclusion (nigamana) must not exceed what the premises establish; (20) abhava (negation/non-existence) has multiple types (absolute/prior/subsequent/locus-specific absence).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Justification is distinct from knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Ten Audi (Western epistemology) observations: (21) justified true belief need not be knowledge (Gettier cases) -- Kernel must handle justified false beliefs differently from knowledge; (22) multiple basic sources of knowledge (perception/memory/introspection/reason/testimony) must not be collapsed; (23) direct (non-inferential) vs indirect (inferential) knowledge must both be handled; (24) justification is prima facie/defeasible (undermining and overriding defeaters); (25) knowledge does not require certainty; (26) internalism vs externalism is a real distinction the Kernel must take a position on; (27) memory preserves but does not create knowledge -- preservation vs generation must be distinguished; (28) testimony transmits knowledge via the attester's knowledge, but testimony-based justification can arise independently; (29) coherence alone is not sufficient for justification; (30) skepticism (hallucination/illusion/dreaming) challenges knowledge claims -- the Kernel must handle uncertainty/fallibility without collapsing into skepticism.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The 10 Strongest Falsification Questions
a_rows_sample.statement: Ten falsification questions posed against any Kernel boundary claim, five from Chinese traditions (how does the Kernel determine a unit of knowledge is no longer 'the same'; how is continuity maintained across change; does naming prescribe or merely label; is context internal or external to a claim's truth; does justification depend on practical consequences) and five from Tarka-Nyaya (does the boundary definition suffer avyapti/ativyapti/asambhava; is every claimed invariant tested in both anvaya and vyatireka directions; what is the counter-correlative if 'retraction does not exist as a Kernel state'; does any claimed capability exceed its premises; has an argument's reason changed shape mid-debate without being recorded).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Names prescribe what things should be, not just name what they are.
a_rows_sample.statement: Five most-surprising observations: normative naming (names prescribe, not just classify); contradictions are not necessarily errors (perspectival difference vs logical inconsistency); absence != withdrawal (a claim no longer existing vs no longer assertable); knowing is becoming, not possessing; the smallest boundary may be defined by what it must NOT include (per Tarka's ativyapti/asambhava tests).

a_rows_sample.anchor: The 5 Observations Most Likely to Be Relevant to a Minimal Knowledge Kernel
a_rows_sample.statement: Five observations ranked most relevant to a minimal Knowledge Kernel: identity is relational not intrinsic; justification is practical (consequence-based, not merely internal-consistency-based); change is continuous (versioning/state management must handle continuous transformation, not just discrete states); context is constitutive (must be internal to knowledge representation, not external metadata); naming is normative (must be handled as part of the knowledge itself).

a_rows_sample.anchor: The Observations That Should NOT Influence Architecture Without Further Evidence
a_rows_sample.statement: Five observations explicitly flagged as not (yet) architecturally actionable: Daoism's claim that 'the Dao that can be named is not the enduring Dao' (not directly relevant -- the kernel must name things regardless); Confucian ritual (li) emphasis (unclear translation to a kernel); Mohism's claim that impartiality requires active effort (ethical claim, unclear architectural implication); 'knowledge changes as it is used' (unclear how to model without further investigation); Tarka's full nigrahasthana catalog (more detailed than a minimal kernel needs -- core attacks on definition/reason/vyapti/fallacious-reason are more immediately applicable).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Questions That Conventional DDD Analysis May Not Expose
a_rows_sample.statement: Ten questions conventional DDD analysis may not expose: whether bounded contexts/boundaries are actually stable or shift with context; whether identity is a relation rather than an aggregate property; whether names are normative rather than stable identifiers; whether contradiction can be a legitimate perspective difference rather than an error; whether justification is fundamentally practical/consequence-based rather than internal; whether context is constitutive of knowledge rather than external; whether knowledge is a capacity ('becoming') rather than a possession; whether absence has multiple types rather than being uniform non-existence; whether 'retraction' is a continuous process rather than a deletion event; whether certainty is required for knowledge at all.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Questions That Chinese Philosophy Does NOT Help Answer
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit scope limitation: Chinese philosophy provides no help on formal modeling, implementation (APIs/data structures/algorithms), performance/scalability/reliability, UX, integration with existing systems, security, data persistence/storage/versioning, distributed-systems/network-topology questions, temporal modeling, or computational complexity -- it offers distinctions and observations, not a modeling language.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Separation of Grounds
a_rows_sample.statement: A four-tier separation-of-grounds discipline is applied throughout: Historically Grounded Observation (direct textual claims from Daodejing/Zhuangzi/Kongzi/Mohist fa/Xunzi/Tarka-sangraha/Audi), Philosophical Interpretation (what those claims imply), Architectural Inference (what a Kernel would need to account for under that interpretation), and Speculation (extensions beyond the source material, e.g. how a Kernel might implement Confucian role-based justification or Daoist continuous transformation) -- kept explicitly distinct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: These are not questions about missing capabilities. They are questions about the assumptions the Kernel makes about the nature of knowledge itself.
a_rows_sample.statement: Final consolidated set of 15 architect-facing questions (naming as neutral vs normative; identity as property vs relation; contradiction as error vs perspective; context as external vs constitutive; justification as claim-property vs practical relationship; retraction as event vs process; transformation as discrete vs continuous; absence as single state vs typed (abhava); knowledge as possession vs capacity; authority as source-property vs relationship; whether boundary reasoning is established via paksa-sadhya-hetu or assumed; whether invariants are tested in both anvaya/vyatireka directions; whether representation is silently converted into truth; whether the knowledge/non-knowledge boundary is stable or provisional; whether impartial evaluation is a default or an active achievement) -- framed explicitly as questions about the Kernel's assumptions about the nature of knowledge itself, not about missing capabilities.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The S1-F018 mapping is no longer merely a candidate... the dilemma therefore demands an external-but-atomic member -- and that is precisely asambhava: a definition describing something that cannot exist under the Constitution. So Session 1's inference is corroborated from a source it did not have... POSSIBLE INDEPENDENT ARRIVAL -- third in the register.
a_rows_sample.statement: S1-F023's self-labelled inference that S1-F018's Entity/Value-Object dilemma is an asambhava case (a definition describing something that cannot exist) is independently corroborated: S2-R-F018.1 established from law (not from the Tarka taxonomy) that the dilemma's option set omits the route the law actually takes -- EvidenceLinks as a bounded Collection of external-content references under C-3 -- which is exactly an external-but-atomic member the dilemma's options cannot represent; recorded as a possible independent arrival (third in the review series's register).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Nyaya treats knowledge as fundamentally relational and process-based, not as a static property of propositions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Three headline findings from applying Nyaya pramana theory, tarka, realism, and debate theory to the Kernel: (1) knowledge is relational/process-based, not a static property -- a claim is knowledge only if generated by the right kind of process (pramana) and defeasible by legitimate doubt; (2) Nyaya's two-tier epistemology (default trust in cognition vs reflective certification when doubt arises) maps onto a 'knowledge core' (trusted default) vs 'adjudication process' (certification) distinction; (3) Nyaya's theory of error is parasitic on truth (error is misplacement of properties onto the wrong object, requiring prior knowledge of the properties/object), directly relevant to the anti-reasoner concept and the representation-!=-truth problem.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Requires Four Factors
b_rows_sample.statement: Ten Nyaya observations (Part 1): (1) knowledge requires four unified factors -- knower, known, knowledge source, and knowledge itself (Nyaya-sutra 1.1.1); (2) error is parasitic on truth, a misplacement of a property onto the wrong object (Nyaya-sutra 4.2.35, the shell/silver example); (3) a two-tier epistemology of default trust vs certification when doubt arises (2.1.20); (4) pramanas (perception/inference/analogy/testimony, 1.1.3) are causes of veridical cognition, not conscious justifications -- a causal account of knowledge; (5) inference (linga) has a three-part perception->recollection->inference structure (1.1.5); (6) vyapti (invariable concomitance) must be tested in both anvaya (positive) and vyatireka (negative) directions (1.1.34); (7) absence (abhava) requires a counter-correlative (pratiyogi), you cannot assert non-existence of X without knowing what X would be if it existed (4.2.33); (8) perception is defined by four conditions (sense-object connection, language-independence, inerrancy, definitiveness, 1.1.4); (9) the lamp analogy is interpreted as mutual certification among pramanas, not self-certification (2.1.19), a coherentist element within Nyaya's foundationalism; (10) doubt (samsaya) is the catalyst for inquiry, not a failure state, arising from five distinct triggers (1.1.23).

b_rows_sample.anchor: The 10 Strongest Falsification Questions from Nyaya
b_rows_sample.statement: Ten falsification questions mirroring the ten observations: definition adequacy (avyapti/ativyapti/asambhava, and whether 'does not depend on language' is even met by a digital system); reason integrity via the five-part pratijna-hetu-udaharana-upanaya-nigamana structure; invariant testing in both anvaya/vyatireka directions; absence-type question for 'retraction'; the five hetvabhasa (pseudo-prover) defects (deviant/contradictory/inconclusive/unproven/mistimed); representation vs truth (viparyaya); whether unknown/doubt/contradiction/error are collapsed into one 'uncertain' state (samsaya); conclusion-excess (nigamana exceeding pratijna+hetu); nigrahasthana argument-integrity checks (proposition/reason changed, meaning shifted); and whether the Kernel distinguishes knowledge by pramana source.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge is a Causal Process, Not a Property
b_rows_sample.statement: Five most-surprising observations: knowledge is generated by a causal process, not possessed as a property (a Kernel might need to track the generation process/pramana, not just the claim); error requires prior knowledge of truth (opposite of the Western default-doubt assumption, so error might be modeled as a modified version of truth, not a separate category); default trust, not skepticism, is Nyaya's epistemic starting point (opposite of the Cartesian default-doubt assumption); absence is a real category with structure (counter-correlative plus type: absolute/prior/subsequent/locus-based); doubt has five distinct causal types, not just confidence degrees.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The 5 Observations Most Likely Relevant to a Minimal Knowledge Kernel
b_rows_sample.statement: Five observations ranked most kernel-relevant: the four-factor knower/known/source/knowledge relational structure (a Kernel storing only propositions loses this structure); the two-tier trusted-vs-certified structure; the parasitism thesis (error as modified truth, not a separate category); the counter-correlative requirement for absence/retraction/deletion; the five distinct doubt types (not just a confidence scalar).

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Debate Framework as Falsification Apparatus
b_rows_sample.statement: Nyaya's three debate types (vada: truth-seeking debate using pramanas/tarka without tricks; jalpa: disputation using equivocation/misleading objections/clinchers; vitanda: destructive debate refuting without establishing) plus the five-component formal demonstration (proposition/reason/illustration/application/conclusion), five pseudo-provers, and twenty-two clinchers (ways to lose an argument) suggest a Kernel 'argument integrity' test checking definitional defects (avyapti/ativyapti/asambhava), reason defects (savyabhicara/viruddha/satpratipaksa/asiddha/badhita), and argument integrity (proposition/reason/meaning changes).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 5 Observations That Should NOT Influence Architecture Without Further Evidence
b_rows_sample.statement: Five Nyaya observations explicitly flagged as not (yet) architecturally actionable: perception-as-inerrant (too specific an epistemological claim); the four metaphysical categories (substance/quality/action/universal); Nyaya's theism (God as causal factor, not relevant to a minimal kernel); the full 22-clincher list (more detail than a minimal kernel needs); Nyaya's realism about universals (jati) as a specific ontological claim.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Questions That Conventional DDD Analysis May Not Expose
b_rows_sample.statement: Ten DDD-blind-spot questions: relational (knower/known/source/knowledge) vs identity-holder aggregates; causal generation vs internal justification; error-as-modified-truth vs error-as-separate-category; absence-requires-counter-correlative vs absence-as-non-existence; five doubt types vs a degree-of-uncertainty scalar; knowledge-as-generated-by-causes vs knowledge-as-possession; perception-as-inerrant-by-definition vs perception-as-fallible; testimony-as-inerrant-when-trustworthy vs testimony-as-fallible; definitions tested for avyapti/ativyapti/asambhava vs definition-as-neutral-act; multi-stage (perception/recollection/reflection) vs linear inference.

b_rows_sample.anchor: These are not questions about missing capabilities. They are questions about the assumptions the Kernel makes about the nature of knowledge itself.
b_rows_sample.statement: Final consolidated ten architect-facing questions restating the Part 1-2 material: default-trust vs mandatory-certification; error as separate category vs modified truth; knowledge as static property vs dynamic knower/known/source/knowledge relationship; absence types requiring a counter-correlative; five doubt types vs a single uncertainty state; self-testing definitions for avyapti/ativyapti/asambhava; distinguishing the generation process (pramana) from the knowledge itself; representing that generation process per unit of knowledge; self-certifying vs mutually-certifying knowledge sources; retraction as discrete deletion vs gradual correction process.
